parole.testo: From Old Spanish -dumne, from Vulgar Latin *-tūm(i)nem, from Latin -tūdinem (apparently via dissimilation/assimilation). Doublet of -itúdine and -itud. Found in both words inherited from Latin (certidumbre, dulcedumbre, mansedumbre, muchedumbre, servidumbre, soledumbre) and words formed within Spani

parole.significato: Suffix indicating the third-person singular indicative preterite of -er and -ir verbs.
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *-īut, from Latin -īvit; compare Portuguese -iu. The shift of stress from the expected *-ío is probably by analogy with the first conjugation equivalent -ó.

parole.significato: first person preterite ending of regular -er and -ir verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *-īī < Latin -īvī, first-person singular present perfect active indicative ending of the fourth conjugation, later generalized to almost all non–first-conjugation verbs.

parole.significato: a suffix indicating the third-person singular indicative preterite of a verb in -ar
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *-āut, from Latin -āvit. Compare Galician and Portuguese -ou.
Vulgar Latin ad vicēs (“at times”). Compare Italian a volte for a similar construction.
Inherited from Old Spanish abaxar. By surface analysis, a- + bajar. Compare English abase.

parole.significato: to embrace (to hold with the arms)
parole.testo: From a variant of abracar, from Vulgar Latin *abbracchicāre, a verb based on Latin bracchium (“arm”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *advannāre (“grade seeds with a sieve”), from Latin ad- + vannare (“winnow, fan”). Doublet of abanar, which was borrowed from Galician or Portuguese.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *betūle or *betūlus, from Latin betulla, diminutive of Gaulish *betua, from Proto-Celtic *betwiyos, *betuyā (“birch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-. The prefix a- is due to the influence of abeto (“fir”). Also compare Catalan bedoll, French bouleau, Portuguese bétula,
Inherited from Old Spanish avismo, from Vulgar Latin *abīsmus, from Late Latin abyssus, from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos, “bottomless”).
Contracted from Vulgar Latin *abbracchicāre, a verb based on Latin bracchium (“arm”).

parole.significato: to hug, to embrace (a person, an animal)
parole.testo: From a- + brazo (“arm”) + -ar. Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + -o.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abbiberāre, ultimately derived from Latin bibere (“drink”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *upupella, diminutive of Latin upupa.
Inherited from Old Spanish avuelo, from Vulgar Latin *av(i)olum, ultimately from Latin avus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abhorriō, from Latin abhorrēre (“to be disinclined to; to abhor”). Cognate with English abhor.
Inherited from Old Spanish avez, from Vulgar Latin *ad vix, from ad + vix. Compare Romanian abia. A less likely theory derives it from Arabic.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. By surface analysis, a- + cabo (“end, conclusion”) + -ar.
Inherited from Old Spanish acaesçer, from a Vulgar Latin verb *accadescere, *accadiscere, from *accadēre, from Latin ad- + cadere. Cf. the attested Classical Latin form accidō, accidere.
Inherited from Old Spanish acatar ("look at closely, consider", later "pay homage to"), from Vulgar Latin *accattāre, from Late Latin cattāre, from Latin captāre. Compare Portuguese acatar.
Inherited from Old Spanish azevo, from Vulgar Latin *acifolium or *acifulum, ultimately from Latin aquifolium.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *oscitiāre, from Latin oscitāre (“gape, yawn, open one's mouth”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, from ad- + Latin colligere (whence Spanish coger).
Inherited from Old Spanish acomparar, from Vulgar Latin *accomparāre.

parole.significato: to come to pass, to happen, to occur, to transpire, to come about, to befall
parole.testo: From a- + Old Spanish contesçer, derived from Old Spanish contir, from Vulgar Latin *contigīre, from Latin contingere. Akin to Portuguese acontecer.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accordāre.
From the obsolete coso (“road, way”), or less likely a Vulgar Latin *accursāre, from Latin cursus. Compare Portuguese acossar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum illāc, from Latin eccum + illāc. Compare Galician and Portuguese acolá; cf. also Asturian acullá.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum hāc. Compare Galician acá, Portuguese cá, Italian qua, French çà and Sicilian ccà.
From earlier delgazar, from Vulgar Latin *delicatiāre, from Latin delicātus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adferrāre, from ferrum (“iron, sword”).
Inherited from Old Spanish afrontar, from Vulgar Latin *affrontāre, derived from Latin ad- + frontem + -āre. Doublet of afrontar. By surface analysis, a- + frente + -ar.

parole.significato: to face, address, tackle, meet, deal with, confront, cope with, handle, bear, manage, (e.g. reality, an issue, a situat…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affrontāre, derived from Latin ad- + frontem. Doublet of afrentar. The expected diphthongization of Latin stressed /ŏ/ is attested in medieval conjugations such as afruenta.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin agustus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eguttāre, from Latin gutta, whence English gout and gutter.
From Vulgar Latin *aggraviāre, from Latin aggravāre. Compare English aggrieve and aggravate.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *acriāre, a causative verb from Latin acer (“sour”).
From aguaza + -ero, from Vulgar Latin *aquacea, from Latin aqua.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aquacea, from Latin aqua. By surface analysis, agua + -aza.

parole.significato: prod, cattle prod (device used to goad animals into moving)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (pertica) *aquīleāta, from *aquīleus, vulgar variant of Latin acūleus (“prick”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aquīleōnem, from *aquīleus, vulgar variant of acūleus (“prick, goad”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *acūtiāre, from Latin acūtus. Compare Catalan agusar, French aiguiser, Italian aguzzare, Occitan agusar, Portuguese aguçar.

parole.significato: to drown (kill by immersion in water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish afogar, from Vulgar Latin *affōcāre, alteration of Latin offōcāre. Compare Portuguese afogar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affundāre, derived from Latin fundus (“bottom”). By surface analysis, a- + hondo + -ar. Compare Portuguese afundar.

parole.significato: to smoke (apply smoke to, for example food)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affūmāre, ultimately from Latin fūmus (“smoke”, noun). By surface analysis, a- + humo + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affugientāre, from Latin fugientem, present participle of fugiō (“flee”).
From older ahajar, from Old Spanish haja, probably from Vulgar Latin *fallia (“defect”), from Latin fallĕre.

From justo. Some of the medieval Old Spanish senses (compare Ladino ajustar (“to add”)) seem to correspond better to Vulgar Latin *adiuxtāre or *iuxtāre, from Latin iuxta (compare French ajouter (“to add”)); compare ayustar.
From Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus.

parole.significato: to reach; to get to to catch up
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *incalciāre (ultimately related to Latin calx (“heel”)), influenced by Latin ad and/or the Spanish preposition al. Compare the form encalzar, Portuguese encalçar, Catalan encalçar. Also compare English causeway, cause- being derived from calciare (“to tread”), which Spanish calzar

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alēnitāre, a metathetic variant of *an(h)ēlitāre, from anhēlitus (“breathe”) + -āre. The diphthongization in rhizotonic conjugations (yo aliento) is etymologically unexpected, considering the Latin /ē/, but may have to do with analogy with other verbs ending in -entar, s
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alicunus, from Latin alĭquis (“someone”) + unus (“one”). Cognate with French aucun, Italian alcuno, Galician algún, Portuguese algum.

Inherited from Old Spanish almendra (compare Ladino almendra), from Vulgar Latin *amendla, *amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē), of Pre-Greek origin. Doublet of amígdala and mandorla.

From Vulgar Latin amidōnem, from Latin amylum, from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon); influenced by words of Arabic derivation beginning al-. Compare French amidon, Greek άμυλο (ámylo), Hebrew עמילן (amilan).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *haemorrheuma, from Ancient Greek αἱμο- (haimo-, “blood”) + ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, flow”), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”). The first syllable was formed by analogy with other Spanish words borrowed from Arabic with the article اَل (al-, “the”). Cognate with Galician almorrá,
Inherited from Old Spanish almuerzo, from Vulgar Latin *admordium, from admordere. Compare Portuguese almoço.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alaudea, from Latin alauda. Related to alondra.

parole.significato: a drink composed of water, honey and spices
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aloxia, variant of Late Latin aloxinum (“hydromel”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alaudula, diminutive form of Latin alauda (compare French alouette, Italian allodola), of Celtic origin. Related to aloja.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alaudea, from Latin alauda. Related to alondra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *admānēscere.

From amenaza (“threat”) + -ar. Alternatively, from a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *admināciāre (“to threaten”) < *mināciāre (“threaten”), from minācia (“threat”). Compare Catalan amenaçar, French menacer, Italian minacciare, Occitan amenaçar, Portuguese ameaçar, Romanian ameninţa, Sicilian amminazzari.
Inherited from Old Spanish amiztad, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, accusative singular of Latin *amīcitas, from amīc- (“friend”) + -tās (abstract noun-forming suffix).
From a- + a variant of muchiguar (also obsolete), from Vulgar Latin *multificāre (“multiply, increase”), from Latin multus (“much”) + -ficāre (factitive verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, derived from Latin amōrem (“love”). By surface analysis, amor + -oso.
Inherited from Old Spanish amparar, emparar, from Vulgar Latin *anteparāre (“to prevent”), from Latin ante- + parō, parāre. Compare Portuguese amparar, Catalan emparar, Occitan aparar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hanca, from Proto-Germanic *hankō (related to *ankijǭ (“joint, limb”)). Cognate with English haunch.
From Old Spanish anciano, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *anteānus.

parole.significato: Older than a year but not much older than two. (of livestock, especially sheep)
parole.testo: Perhaps from an earlier *anozgo, from a Vulgar Latin *annoticus, with change of suffix from Latin annotinus (whence Romanian noaten (“yearling sheep”)).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *andagĭne. Possibly from Latin indāgō (“encirclement”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adnecāre, prefixed from Latin necāre (“murder”). The verb's sense specialized to 'drown' throughout Romance; compare French noyer, Italian annegare, Romanian îneca, Portuguese anegar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hamiceolus, diminutive of hamus, whence Spanish hamo.

parole.significato: to evil-eye (cast an evil eye upon)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adoculāre, from oclus, from Latin oculus. Cognate with Galician ollar, Mirandese oulhar, Portuguese olhar, and Italian adocchiare.

parole.significato: to extinguish (a flame, fire), to douse
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appācāre, from Latin ad- + pācāre. Compare to English apay.
From Vulgar Latin *appedare, from Latin ad pedem.
From Vulgar Latin *appicāre, from Latin picāre (“smear with pitch”), from pix (“pitch”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad poenam, with an additional adverbial /-s/ (compare mientras < Latin dum interim).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appārium, ultimately from Latin pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: to feel like; to fancy; would like; to be down for
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appetēscere, from Latin appetere. Compare English appetize and English appetite.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appositāre, from Latin appositus.

parole.significato: to gather sheep into a sheepfold
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appressicāre, from Latin appressus, participle of apprimō, from premō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, a compound of Latin eccum and ille.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum inde, from Latin eccum + inde. Cognate with Portuguese aquém and Italian quindi.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc, from eccum (“this”) + hīc (“here”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin arger, argerem, variant of Latin agger.
From a Vulgar Latin *ardibundus, from Latin ārdeō + -bundus.

Inherited from Old Spanish arquero, possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin *arcārius, alteration of arcuārius, from Latin arcus (“bow”). Analyzable as arco (“bow”) + -ero. Sense "goalkeeper" derived from arco (“goal”) + -ero
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arradicāre (compare Portuguese arraigar, Galician arraigar), from Latin radicāre, from rādīcō (“to take root”). By surface analysis, a- + raigar.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *arredāre (“arrange, provide”), from Gothic *𐍂𐌴𐌸𐍃 (*rēþs, “advice”). Cognate with English array.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arruborare, from Latin rubārī (“redness”).

parole.significato: to make something/someone numb with cold
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin arrigēscĕre (“to become stiff”), from Latin arrigĕre (“raise; rouse, excite”). According to Coromines and Pascual, this infinitive arrecir "barely exists" (apenas existe), and prefer to link the adjective arrecido to a supposed verb *arreeçer, of the same etymology, cognate with Ga
Inherited from Old Spanish arriedro, from Vulgar Latin *ad retrō.

parole.significato: to tuck in; hike up (a skirt, dress)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish arregaçar, from a- + regaçar, from Vulgar Latin *recaptiāre.

From a- + Old Spanish repentirse, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre. The Old Spanish form with /t/ appears to have been influenced by Old French repentir or, less likely, Latin. The expected outcome with voiced /d/, namely rependirse, is also a
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre (see there for more), possibly via a Gallo-Romance intermediate, hence the lack of diphthongization in rhizotonic conjugations.

parole.significato: to throw, to hurl, to toss, to fling (cause an object to move rapidly through the air)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrot(u)lāre, *rotulāre, from Latin rotāre (“to turn, to wheel”). The lack of diphthongization (**arruejo) is due to the palatalization of the -tl- > -cl- cluster to [ʎ], then Old Spanish [ʒ], raising the previous vowel to close [o] — compare Latin oculus, which gave ris

Inherited from Old Spanish arzon~arçon, from Vulgar Latin *arciōnem (“saddlebow”), from Latin arcus (“bow”). The frequent voiced /dz/ in Old Spanish may be due to the influence of arzen (modern arcén).

Per Roberts, probably inherited from Old Spanish usgo (“disgust”), back-formed from *osgar (“to loathe”), from Vulgar Latin *ōsicō, from Latin ōsus, perfect passive participle of ōdī (“to hate”), with influence from asqueroso. An alternative hypothesis derives this word from Latin eschăra (“scab, sc
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assediāre or *assedeāre, from Latin assidēre. Compare English assess, Romanian așeza.

parole.significato: to secure (to make fast; to close or confine effectually)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish assegurar, from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrare, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe”). Compare English assure.
From Vulgar Latin *(as)similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, a- + semejar. Compare Portuguese assemelhar. Doublet of asimilar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *haspa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *escharōsus (“full of crusts or scabs, scabby”), from Late Latin eschara (“crust, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “scab left from a burn”).

parole.significato: partition wall or other means of enclosure
parole.testo: By surface analysis, atajado + -izo, perhaps corresponding to a- + Vulgar Latin *taliātīcius, from Latin taliāre (“cut”).

parole.significato: to correspond, to concern, to have to do with
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *attangere, variant of Latin attingere.
Inherited from Old Spanish testiguar, from Vulgar Latin *testificāre, from Latin testificārī.

parole.significato: to stir, fan, poke, rouse, stoke
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *attītiāre, derived from Latin tītiō (“firebrand”). Compare Portuguese atiçar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tussicāre (“to cough, become fatigued”), a diminutive of Latin tussio (“to cough”).
Inherited from Old Spanish atras (“behind”) from Vulgar Latin *ad trans, from Latin trāns (“beyond”).

Inherited from Old Spanish, from an older *ullar, from Vulgar Latin *ūl(ŭ)lāre, from Latin ululāre, ultimately from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root. Doublet of the borrowed ulular. Cognate with English ululate.
Perhaps from the base *aut, imitative of its call, + -illo. Or, from Vulgar Latin *ōtellus, a diminutive of Ancient Greek ὠτός (ōtós), genitive of οὖς (oûs, “ear”), referring to its ears.
From Vulgar Latin *adventura, from Late Latin adventurus, from Latin advenire, adventum (“to arrive”). Cognate with English adventure.

From a Vulgar Latin *advitiāre (“accustom, habituate, familiarize”), from Latin vitium. Compare Italian avvezzare, Portuguese vezar, avezar, Provençal Occitan avezar, envezar, Catalan avesar, cf. also Romanian învăța.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *iaiūnāre, present active infinitive of *aiūnō, iaiūnō, from Late Latin ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus. Compare English jejune.

Inherited from Old Spanish ayuno, from a Vulgar Latin *aiūnus < *iaiūnus, jajūnus, from Latin iēiūnus, from Proto-Italic *jagjūnos, itself from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-, adjectival form of *Hyeh₂ǵ-ye/o- (“to sacrifice”).
Inherited from Old Spanish açada, from Vulgar Latin *asciāta, from Latin ascia. Compare Portuguese enxada and Catalan aixada.
From Old Spanish aztor, adtor, from Vulgar Latin *acceptor, replacement of Latin accipiter. For the simplification of the cluster, compare rezar from recitāre and plazo from placitum.
From Old Spanish eñadir, inherited from Vulgar Latin *innaddere, from Latin in- (“into”) + addere (“to add”).

parole.significato: aged (of food, particularly wine, but also cheese or alcoholic spirits such as rum)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *anniclus, syncopated form of Latin anniculus (“one-year-old”). Cf. also añojo, which derives from a variant form and preserves the meaning more closely.

parole.significato: a young bull between one and two years old
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *annuclu < *annuculus, variant of anniculus (cf. also añejo (“aged”), which took on a different meaning).
From the hypothesized Vulgar Latin *baba (“drooling, infantile talk”), ultimately imitative of children's speech on the pattern of the repeated syllable ba.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bat(t)uāculum, from Latin bat(t)uere (“beat”). Compare Portuguese badalo.

parole.significato: shovel, specifically one used to pick up ashes in fireplaces and braziers
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish badil, from Vulgar Latin *batīle, from Latin batillum.
Inherited from Old Spanish baxar, from Vulgar Latin *bassiāre, from Late Latin bassus.

Inherited from Old Spanish baladrar (c. 1270), from Vulgar Latin *balatrare, related to Latin balatrō (“clown, charlatan”). By surface analysis, baladro (“scream”) + -ar. Cognate with Galician bradar, Portuguese bradar, Catalan baladrejar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *barbūtus (“bearded”). Compare Portuguese barbudo, Italian barbuto, French barbu. By surface analysis, barba (“beard”) + -udo.
Inherited from Old Spanish barro, from Vulgar Latin *barrum (“clay, mud”), from Paleo-Hispanic or Iberian; compare Middle Irish broch (“waste, dregs”) and Gaulish *barros (“the bushy end”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastō, possibly borrowed from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to carry, bear (weight)”).

Inherited from Old Spanish vassura, from Vulgar Latin *versūra, ultimately derived from Latin verrō (“sweep”). Unrelated to Latin versūra (“refinancing”), which derives from vertō (“turn”). Compare typologically Proto-Slavic *sъmetь, *sъmetьje (whence Polish śmieć, Serbo-Croatian смеће), akin to *me

parole.significato: to bathe (to clean a person by immersion in water or using water; to give someone a bath)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *baneare, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare Portuguese banhar, Catalan banyar, French baigner, Italian bagnare.

parole.significato: any puffball mushroom of the Lycoperdon genus
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vissīnum, derived from Latin vissīre (“to pass wind”). Cf. the other name for this mushroom, pedo de lobo (“lit. ‘wolf's fart’”).
Inherited from Old Spanish verça, from a Vulgar Latin *virdia (see for cognates), from syncopation of viridis (“green”).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *baisu(m), from Latin bāsium.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bīstius, a masculine form of bīstia, from Latin bēstia (“beast”). Compare English beast. Compare with the inherited doublet bicha and the direct borrowing bestia.

Inherited from Old Spanish bien venido, inherited from Vulgar Latin *bene venītus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, bien (“well”

Inherited from Old Spanish bigornia, bicornia, from a Vulgar Latin *bicŏrnĭa (“anvil”), from Latin bicornis (“two-horned”) nominalized in the feminine with -a. Cognate with Galician bigorna, French bigorne, early modern Italian bicornia, Andalusian, Moroccan and Algerian Arabic بقرنية (buqurnīya).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin bīnāre (“to do something twice; to work the land twice”), from a derivative of Latin bīnī, from bis (“twice, two times”). Cognate with French biner (“to hoe”).
From Vulgar Latin pirulus, from pirum (“pear”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *verrea, from Latin verres (“boar”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *versicus, itself from Latin versus (“turned”). Cognate with Asturian viesgu and Portuguese vesgo.

Cross of lobagante (which is from Vulgar Latin *lucopante, from Ancient Greek λυκοπάνθηρος (lukopánthēros, “snow leopard”) because of the fierce appearance of its large claws) with bogar (from Latin vocāre (“to call”)) and avante (from Latin ab + ante).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bonacia, alteration of malacia. Compare Italian bonaccia (“dead calm”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bulbulliāre.

parole.significato: tassel (ball-shaped bunch of plaited or otherwise entangled threads)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *burrula, diminutive of Late Latin burra. Compare Portuguese borla.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin *borrasicare, from Late Latin borrās (“north wind”), from Ancient Greek Βορρᾶς (Borrhâs). Cognate with Latin boreās from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās) (Old Attic/Doric), and with English boreal.

parole.significato: person who watches over the cows
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish boyarizo, from Vulgar Latin *bovāricius, from Latin bovem (“cow”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Possibly; or from; modificatore <unc> nel legame
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish bravo, possibly from Vulgar Latin *bravus or *brabus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus (or from metathesis of an intermediate form *babru-).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vertiāre, from Latin vertĕre (“to turn”). Doublet of verter (“to pour, spill”).
Inherited from Old Spanish breço, from Vulgar Latin *broccium.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brigna, perhaps from a Gaulish *brignā, from Proto-Celtic *brixs (“hill”).

parole.significato: hoarse, raspy, harsh, coarse, rough, uncouth, wild, untamed
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin bruncus, possibly a cross of broccus (“having projecting teeth”) and truncus (“trunk”).

Inherited from Old Spanish buey, from Vulgar Latin *boem for Latin bovem (compare Italian bue), accusative singular of bōs. The variants güey and wey represent a neutralization of the clusters /bw/ and /gw/. Doublet of bife.
From Vulgar Latin *buxita, from Latin buxis. Compare English box.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *burius, whence Italian buio.

Uncertain. The Real Academia Española suggests Vulgar Latin *burrula, from burrae, from Late Latin burra (“trifles; nonsense, trickery”) (compare, however, borla, which would be a doublet). Also see Italian burla. Possibly a cognate with English bureau.

parole.significato: arch (arch-shaped arrangement of trapezoidal stones, designed to redistribute downward force outward, or other similar…
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *volvita, alteration of Latin volūta, from volvere (“turn”), but this presents serious phonetic difficulties. Compare Portuguese abóbada. More likely of Germanic origin, from a Gothic *𐌱𐌿𐍅𐌹𐌸𐌰 (*buwiþa), from a derivative of Proto-Germanic *būaną (“to dwell reside, build”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capillūtus. By surface analysis, cabello + -udo.
Inherited from Old Spanish cabeça, from Vulgar Latin capitia, from the neuter plural (reanalyzed as a feminine singular) of Latin capitium, diminutive of caput.

From Vulgar Latin *cāvicula, from Latin clāvicula (“pin”); probably via Old Occitan cavilla. Cognate with Italian caviglia, Portuguese cavilha, Occitan cavilha. Doublet of llavija, lavija, clavija, and clavícula. First attested in 1489.

parole.significato: end, edge, extremity (furthest or terminal point of something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput-. Doublet of jefe and chef.
From Vulgar Latin *capreus, from Latin caper. Compare Portuguese caibro, cf. also French chevron.

Inherited from Old Spanish cabrito. Analyzable as cabra (“goat”) + -ito; may have originally corresponded to a Vulgar Latin or Late Latin caprītus (attested in Salic Law), as the perfect passive participle of a verb *caprīre (“give birth (of goats)”), from Latin caper (which would have normally yiel

parole.significato: piece of the handle of a knife
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capla, contracted form of Late Latin capula, plural of capulum (“hilt”), from Latin capiō.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin *cacclus < *cacculus, from Latin cāccabus (“pot”), see also Galician cacho (“broken container, broken piece of a container”) and Portuguese caco (“piece of pottery”). Compare also Italian cacchio.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cattulus, from Latin catulus (“whelp”).

Inherited from Old Spanish cachondo (mid-13th c. in Libro de los animales que caçan), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *cattulibundus, from catuliō (“to be on heat”) or catulus (“whelp”) + -bundus. Equivalent to cacho (“chub”) + -ondo.

Uncertain. Likely inherited from Vulgar Latin *cattulus, from Latin catŭlus (“whelp, puppy”), plus the suffix -orro; whence also Portuguese cachorro. If so, a doublet of cacho (“chub”). An alternative link to Basque txakur, xakur (“puppy”) has been proposed, but it is often dismissed as speculative.

Inherited from Old Spanish cadera (“chair, throne”), from Vulgar Latin cathégra (attested in Pompeiian inscriptions), variant of Latin cathedra (“armchair”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “chair”). Doublet of cátedra. Compare Portuguese cadeira (“chai
Inherited from Vulgar Latin cals, from Latin calx (via the nominative), from Ancient Greek χάλιξ (khálix, “pebble”).
From Vulgar Latin *calandria, from Ancient Greek κάλανδρος (kálandros, “lark”).

From obsolete calaño (“of the same quality”), ultimately from Latin quālis, possibly by way of hypothetical Vulgar Latin *quālāneus or by the influence of Spanish tamaño (“size”). If so, equivalent to cuál + -aña.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calidizāre.

parole.significato: to heat, to warm up (cause an increase in temperature)
parole.testo: From caliente + -ar, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *calentāre. Compare Portuguese aquentar, Galician quentar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *callāre, from Latin chalāre, from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō). Compare Portuguese calar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *callicula.; compare attested Late Latin calliculus. By surface analysis, calle + -eja.
Inherited from Old Spanish calçada, itself from Vulgar Latin *calciāta (“paved road”), feminine of calciātus (“paved with limestone”), ultimately from Latin calx (“pebble”).

parole.significato: to change, to shift, to switch, to alter
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin cambiāre, from change in conjugation of cambīre, of Gaulish origin. Probably through Asturian cambiar, Galician cambiar or Aragonese cambiar, given the conservation of mb group. Compare also the probable native variant Old Spanish form came

Inherited from Old Spanish camello, from Vulgar Latin *camēllus, from Latin camēlus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *gamal-. More at camel. Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, camino + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cannastra, from Latin canistrum. Cognate with English canister.
Probably from Latin canīcula (through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *canicla, later becoming an adjective of both genders). Doublet of canícula.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *canīle, derived from Latin canis (“dog”). By surface analysis, can + -il.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *chamaethusius, from Ancient Greek χαμαί (khamaí, “on the earth, ground”) and θύος (thúos, “burnt offering”), meaning "incense of the earth".
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cappāre, derivative of *cappō, from Latin cāpō.
From Vulgar Latin capischolus, from Latin caput scholae (“head of the school, principal”).
From a Vulgar Latin root *cappō, *cappōnem, from Latin cāpō. Compare Catalan capó, English capon, French chapon, Italian cappone, Portuguese capão.

The etymology is uncertain, but the most plausible source on the basis of both semantics and historical phonology appears to be unattested Vulgar Latin *c(h)araculum (“stick, rod”), which would have been a Latinized diminutive of Ancient Greek χάραξ (khárax, “stick”), whence also χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr

parole.significato: any of a number of plants. See Spanish Wikipedia
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cardincula, from Latin carduus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carēscere, from Latin carēre (“to lack”), whence English caret. Compare parecer from Vulgar Latin parēscere, from Latin parere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carnūtus, derived from Latin carnem (“meat”). By surface analysis, carne + -udo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cariunculus, from Latin cariēs (“decay”).

parole.significato: lane (a lengthwise division of roadway intended for a single line of vehicles)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish carril, from Vulgar Latin *carrīlis, an alteration of Late Latin currīlis with influence of carrus. Equivalent to carro + -il.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cariceus, from Latin carex.
Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *carōnia. First attested in 1601, and on that basis - considering as well as the lack of an outcome like *carrueña - probably borrowed from Italian carogna.

From archaic carámbalo, from a hypothetical Old Spanish *caramblo, from a Vulgar Latin root *calamulus, diminutive of Latin calamus (“reed, stalk”) [whence English calamari, calumet and calamine], from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos).
From Old Spanish cascar, caxcar, from Vulgar Latin *quassicāre, frequentative of Latin quassāre (“strike”). Doublet of quejar. Cognate with English quash.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *caiātus, from Late Latin caia (“staff”).
Inherited from Old Spanish caçar, from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus. Compare Portuguese caçar and English chase and catch (whence Spanish cachar).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cannabāceus, from Late Latin cannabum (“hemp”).

Inherited from Old Spanish ezebra, of uncertain origin. Likely from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin equiferus (“wild horse”), from equus (“horse”) + ferus (“wild”), possibly through another Romance language first. Compare Portuguese zebra.
From Vulgar Latin *sicciālis, from siccus (“dry”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *siccīna (“jerky”), from Latin siccus (“dry”).
Inherited from Old Spanish cedra (c. 1200), from Vulgar Latin citera, from Latin cithara. Doublet of cítola, cítara, and guitarra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cessiāre, modification of Latin cessāre, whence also Spanish cesar (“cease”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *caenicōsus, from Vulgar Latin *caenica, from Latin caenum (“slime, filth”).
Inherited from Old Spanish ceniza, from Vulgar Latin *cinisia, from Latin cinis. Compare Portuguese cinza and Romanian cenușă.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cercedula, from Latin querquedula (“teal”).
Inherited from Old Spanish cereso, probably from a Vulgar Latin cereseum, from Latin cerasus, from Ancient Greek κερασός (kerasós). Cognate with English cerise and cherry.

parole.significato: an alkaline solution (often made with lye or lime) in which maize grains have been cooked during nixtamalization; remai…
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *cinerata, from Latin cinis (“cold ashes”). Cognate with Galician cernada, Galician cenrada, Portuguese cenrada, Italian cenerata
Inherited from Vulgar Latin cernicula, from cerniculum, from Latin cernō. Cognate with Portuguese cernelha and Galician cernella.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *serracula, from *serraculum, from Late Latin serrō, serrāre (“to close, shut”) (whence serrar, cerrar). Compare with Galician zarralla (“lock”).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, cross-bar”). Compare English serry/serried.

From a modification of Old Spanish berrojo (influenced by the verb cerrar (“to close”)), from Vulgar Latin *verruculum, from Latin vericulum, diminutive of verū (“dart”). Compare the development of Portuguese ferrolho.

parole.significato: to submerge the head of someone or somebody
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subputeāre, a verb formed on Latin sub (“under”) + puteus (“well, pit, dungeon”).
Inherited from Old Spanish chiflar, from a Vulgar Latin *sīfilāre, as a variant of Latin sībilāre. Doublet of silbar.

parole.significato: to shriek, to screech, to scream
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish chirlar, from *chislar, from Vulgar Latin *cistulāre, an alteration of Latin fistulāre (“to play the flute”), which is derived from Latin fistula (“flute”). Compare Catalan xisclar.

parole.significato: A poplar tree, often the black poplar (Populus nigra)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, possibly through an earlier form *llopo, from Vulgar Latin *plōppus, with metathesis from Latin pōpulus. Likely influenced by Portuguese choupo, if not simply borrowed from it.

parole.significato: north-west wind in the Ebro valley
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish çierço, sierço, cierço, from Vulgar Latin cercius, circius.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cicār(r)a, from Latin cicāda. Doublet of chicharra (via Mozarabic).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cingla, syncopated form of Latin cingula. Doublet of cencha. Cf. also the related cincho.
Inherited from Old Spanish çinco, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, from Latin quīnque. Doublet of ponche and ponzu.
Alteration of earlier ciénega, from Vulgar Latin *caenica, from Latin caenum (“silt”).
From Vulgar Latin *cuacula
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cuperāre (“take, seize”), a back-formation from Latin recuperāre (“recover, regain”), whence Spanish recobrar. Doublet of recuperar, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coquīnārium, or a later formation corresponding to cocina + -ero. Doublet of coquinario.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cutisus, from Latin cytisus, from Ancient Greek κύτισος (kútisos). Doublet of cítiso.
From a Vulgar Latin *cōtōnem, derived from Latin cōtem.
From an earlier *cohorzar, from Vulgar Latin confortiare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cuculliāta (“hooded, cowled”), from cuculliō (“hood”), from Latin cucullus (“covering for the head; hood, cowl”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōnfectāre, frequentative of Latin cōnficiō, through its past participle cōnfectus. Compare Portuguese confeitar, Italian confettare and English confect.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōleūtus, derived from Latin cōleus (“testicle”). Compare Portuguese colhudo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla). Cognate to Portuguese cola, Italian colla, French colle.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *colātīcius, from Latin colāre. By surface analysis, colado + -izo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin caulicla < *caulicula, from Latin cauliculus.

Inherited from Old Spanish colmena, from Vulgar Latin *colmēna, probably a borrowing from a Hispano-Celtic language, from Proto-Celtic *kolmēnā, from *kolmos (“straw”) + *-īnā (relational suffix). Doublet of cuelmo (“torch”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin columellus (“canine tooth, tusk”) (attested in Isidore of Seville), masculine variant of columella (literally “small column, pillar”), diminutive of columna (“column”). Used Classically to refer to the grinding teeth of horses in Varro and Pliny in the form columellārēs d
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō.

Inherited from Old Spanish començar, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, from com- + Latin initiāre. Did not show diphthongized conjugations in early medieval texts; their later appearance seems to reflect analogy with the synonym empezar.
Inherited from Old Spanish comer, from Vulgar Latin *comēre, restructuring of Latin comedere.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *compatiscere, from Latin compati.
Inherited from Old Spanish companna, from Vulgar Latin *compānia, from Late Latin compāniō from cum + pānis (“bread”). Compare Galician compaña and Portuguese companha.

parole.significato: to buy (to obtain in exchange of money or goods)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”), whence also Portuguese comprar, Italian comprare, Romanian cumpăra.
From Latin cum + Vulgar Latin nōscum.
From a Vulgar Latin root *conquerīre, from Latin conquīrere (compare Occitan conquerir, French conquérir, Romanian cuceri).

parole.significato: to achieve, succeed in, reach, accomplish, attain
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish conseguir, from Vulgar Latin *cōnsequiō or *cōnsequō, from Latin cōnsequor.

parole.significato: division in the city of Siena
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *contrāta.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *convitāre, from Latin invītāre (“to invite”).

parole.significato: A set of hides or skins from certain animals, especially from bulls, cows, oxen or goats.
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coriāmen.
Inherited from Old Spanish coraçon, from Vulgar Latin *corāceōnem, derived from Latin cor.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cordārium (“late-born lamb”), from Latin chordus (“late-born”). Replaced older año from Latin agnus, which had clashed with the word for "year".
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corniclus < *corniculus, itself a diminutive of Latin cornus.

Probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *carylium, *carulium, diminutive of Latin caryon, from Ancient Greek κάρυον (káruon, “nut”). Cognate with Italian gheriglio. Doublet of carozo, which was inherited via a different development.
From Vulgar Latin *currale (“place for keeping a chariot”), from currus (“chariot”). Compare Portuguese curral.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *curriticium, from Latin currere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin curtius, from Latin curtus (“short”).
Inherited from Old Spanish coser, from Vulgar Latin *cōsēre, from Latin cōnsuere. Cognate with English couture and accoutre/accouter.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *costella, equivalent to costa + -illa, diminutive of costa (“rib”). Compare Catalan costella, Italian costola.
Inherited from Old Spanish costura, from Vulgar Latin *cōnsūtūra, from Latin cōnsuō (“to sew together”) + -tūra (action noun suffix).

parole.significato: coto, half-palm (a traditional unit of length equivalent to about 10.4 cm)
parole.testo: Supposedly a variant of codo (“Spanish cubit”), via Old Spanish cobdo and other Vulgar Latin forms of Latin cubitum (“elbow, Roman cubit”), but more probably a development of or influenced by Latin quārtus (“a fourth”) from its use as a fourth of the cubit or Latin quattuor (“four”) from its approxi

parole.significato: a type of strap or lash
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish coyunda, from Vulgar Latin *conjungula, from Latin conjungō + -ula. For a similar development, see sendos.

parole.significato: to creak, to crack (high-pitched, sharp sound)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cruxir, from Vulgar Latin *cruscīre, from Frankish *krustijan. Compare Catalan cruixir, Old French croissir.

Inherited from Old Spanish quajar, from Vulgar Latin *coaglāre/ *quaglāre, from syncopation of Latin coāgulāre. Doublet of coagular, a borrowing. Compare Aragonese cuallar, Asturian cuayar, Catalan quallar, Galician callar, French cailler.

Possibly from Vulgar Latin *colmos, borrowed from a Hispano-Celtic language, from Proto-Celtic *kolmos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱélh₂m̥. Doublet of colmo (“thatch”). RAE proposes culmus as the origin, but that represents phonetic difficulties as the expected outcome is colmo (mentioned before).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *contu(s) / *comptu(s), from Latin computus. Doublet of cómputo, a borrowing.

parole.significato: snake, serpent (legless reptile of the sub-order Serpentes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish culuebra, from Vulgar Latin *colobra, from Classical Latin colubra. Cognate with Portuguese cobra.

parole.significato: to fulfil, to fulfill, to meet, to deliver (e.g., requirements, prerequisites, promise, vow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cumplir~complir, from Vulgar Latin *complīre, from Latin complēre. The retention of /pl/ is unusual and perhaps reflects some form of conservative tendency. Inherited from Vulgar Latin *contriō, *conteriō, from Latin conterō (“to grind”).

Inherited from Old Spanish camara, borrowed from Vulgar Latin camara, variant of Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “something with an arched cover, a vaulted chamber”). Doublet of cambra.
From Vulgar Latin *gambarus, from Latin gammarus, cammarus (“lobster”), from Ancient Greek κάμμαρος (kámmaros).

parole.significato: bark from a bush or tree
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin reconstructed as *quassicāre (“to strike repeatedly”), from Latin quassāre (“to tremor; to cause to tremor by repeated strikes”) + -icō (suffix indicating frequent or repetitive action), from quatiō (“to shake”) + -tō (suffix indicating frequent or repetitive action). From Vulgar Latin *codicus, from Latin caudex. Cognate with English code.
From Old Spanish dançar, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, from Latin dēcidere.

parole.significato: straight (not crooked or bent; having a constant direction throughout its length)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus, from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of directo.
Inherited from Old Spanish dereçar, from Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre.
From a Vulgar Latin *dērēnicāre, from Latin rēnem. Compare Galician derrear, Romanian dărâna, Old Italian direnare.

parole.significato: to bring down, to shoot down
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *derīpāre, from Latin rīpa (“riverbank”), whence English river.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dērūpāre, from rūpēs (“cliff, rock”), with influence from romper (“to break”). Cognate with Portuguese derrubar (“to overthrow, to destroy, to knock down”) and with Spanish derrubio (“debris, deposit”).
From des- + amparar (“to safeguard”), from Vulgar Latin *anteparāre (“to prevent”).

From des- + ayunar, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *disieiunāre, from Late Latin ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus. Compare English dine, Catalan dejunar, French déjeuner / dîner, Italian digiunare, Occitan dejunar, Portuguese desjejuar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *discaballicāre. By surface analysis, des- + cabalgar.

From Vulgar Latin *disdignāre, reshaping of Latin dēdignārī (“disdain, scorn”) Cognates with English disdain, Portuguese desdenhar, Italian disdegnare and French dédaigner. From the noun deseo; cf. Latin dēsīderō, dēsīderāre (“long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”). Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin verb *dēsidiāre, itself perhaps a crossing between Latin dēsīderāre and invidiāre, from invidia. Compare Portuguese desejar, Catalan desitjar.
From des- + menuzar (obsolete), from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, from Latin minūtus.
Inherited from Old Spanish desfollar, from Vulgar Latin *exfollāre, from Latin follis (“bellows (device), leather bag”).

From despierto (“awake”) + -ar, or it may correspond to a Vulgar Latin *expertāre, from *expertus, from Latin experrēctus (“awoken”), perfect passive participle of expergīscor (“to awake, to wake up”). Cognate with Galician despertar, espertar, Catalan despertar, Portuguese despertar, and Walloon di
Inherited from Old Spanish depues (modified by analogy with des), from Vulgar Latin dē post.

parole.significato: to shatter; to rip to shreds
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *distritiāre, from Latin dis- + trītus + -āre. By surface analysis, des- + trizar.
From Vulgar Latin *depānātōria, from Vulgar Latin *depānāre. By surface analysis, from devanar + -dera.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēpānāre, from Latin pānus (“thread wound upon the bobbin”). Compare Portuguese dobar, Catalan and Occitan debanar, Italian dipanare, Sardinian demanare, Romanian depăna.

Inherited from Old Spanish dinero, from Vulgar Latin *dīnārius, an alteration of Latin dēnārius. Coromines and Pascual explain the /i/ as the result of influence from Byzantine Greek δηνάριον (dinárion). Compare Portuguese dinheiro, Catalan diner, Old Venetan dinaro.

Perhaps from older desfrezar (“to disguise”), from dis- (“removal, away, apart”) + frezar, from Vulgar Latin *frictiāre (“to scrub”), frequentative of fricō (“to rub”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- (“cut, break”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dominiāre, from Latin dominus.

parole.significato: maid, maiden, damsel (girl or an unmarried young woman)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *domnicella (compare Old Occitan donçela, Portuguese donzela, French demoiselle), based on Latin domina (“lady, mistress”). Doublet of damisela.

Inherited from Old Spanish dia, from Vulgar Latin *dia, first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin diēs, from Proto-Italic *djous, from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Compare Old Occitan dia and Old Galician-Portuguese dia. Not cognate with English day.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *iectus, from Latin iactus. Doublet of jeito.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbarricāre, from Latin in- + Vulgar Latin *barra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *invādīre, from Latin invādere. Doublet of invadir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *impediscere, from Latin impedīre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, from Latin prehendere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incaballicāre.
From en- + cadena (“chain”) + -ar. Possibly also corresponds to Vulgar Latin incatēnāre, from Latin catēnāre. Compare Catalan encadenar, Portuguese encadear, French enchaîner, Italian incatenare.

parole.significato: to chase; to give chase to; to dog
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *incalciare, *incalceāre, from Latin calcem (“heel”). Compare English hot on someone's heels. Cognate with Catalan and Portuguese encalçar, Italian incalzare.
From Vulgar Latin hanc hōram (“at this hour”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre. By surface analysis, en- + cargar. Compare Italian incaricare, Portuguese encarregar.
From en- + cenagar, from Vulgar Latin *caenicō, from Latin caenum (“mud”).

parole.significato: holm oak, live oak, evergreen oak
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish enzina, from Vulgar Latin ilicīna, based on Latin īlex (“holm oak”). Compare Asturian ardina or Catalan alzina (“holm oak”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indēbilis, from Latin dēbilis.
From endrina (“sloe, blackthorn”), from earlier andrina, from Iberian Vulgar Latin *ādrīna, evolution of *ātrīna (“black plum”), from Classical Latin āter (“black”).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus. Doublet of junípero, a learned borrowing, and ginebra.

From earlier aneldo, inherited from Old Spanish aneldo, from Vulgar Latin *anēthulum (after metathesis), diminutive of Latin anēthum, from Ancient Greek ἄνηθον (ánēthon). Cognate with Portuguese endro.
Inherited from Old Spanish enemiztat, enemiztad, evolution of Vulgar Latin *inimīcitātem, from Latin inīmicus, based on inimīcitia. Compare Portuguese inimizade.

Attested since 1171. From Old Spanish janero, jenero, from Vulgar Latin ienuārius, from Classical Latin Iānuārius (“(month) of Janus”), from Iānus (“Roman god of doorways”), from iānua (“passage”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“to go”) or Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂-; cf. Sanskrit यान (yāna). Cogn

parole.significato: to trick, to deceive, to hoodwink, to cheat
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (attested in a gloss), from Latin ganniō. Compare Portuguese enganar, Catalan enganyar, Romanian îngâna, Italian ingannare. Cf. also Medieval Latin (in)gannatura (“mockery”).

With the addition of a prefix en-, from a supposed original Old Spanish form *exalbegar (attested later in various altered forms such as axalvegar, jalbegar, xabelgar, etc.), from a Vulgar Latin *exalbicāre, from Latin albus.
Inherited from Old Spanish enxaguar (with metathesis of /w/), from Vulgar Latin *exaquāre (+ the Spanish prefix en-), a verb based on Latin ex- (“out”) + aqua (“water”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *īnsāniāre, from īnsānia (“craziness”), from sānus (“sane”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (found also in Medieval Latin, per Du Cange), from Latin signāre.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin insomnium, from Latin somnium or more likely from en- + sueño. Doublet of insomnio.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put into earth”), from Latin terra.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *intortiliāre, from tortilis. Compare Catalan entortellar, French entortiller.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *invirdēscō. By surface analysis, en- + verde + -ecer.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *involtus, from *involvitus or *involŭtus, for Latin involūtus.
From Vulgar Latin *aequilībrāre.

Inherited from Old Spanish erzer, from Vulgar Latin *ergere, from Latin ērigere. The modern Spanish verb was rebuilt based on the conjugation yergo (“I raise”, from Vulgar Latin *ergō), hence the other inflexions all having /ɡ/ rather than /θ/.
