From Vulgar Latin *exvarāre, from Latin ex- + vārus (“bent outwards”). Compare Asturian esbariar, Galician esvarar and dialectal Catalan esvarar.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Possibly from or linked to a Vulgar Latin *squaleus, from Latin squāleō or squālus. Cf. also Portuguese escalho, escalheiro, Asturian escayu, Romanian scai.
Inherited from Old Spanish escalfar, from Vulgar Latin *excalfare, from Classical Latin excalfacere. Equivalent to es- + calfar. Cognate with English chafe.
Inherited from Old Spanish escapar, from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, from Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

Inherited from Old Spanish escaravayo (with the ending replaced by the pejorative -ajo), from Vulgar Latin *scarafaius (cf. Italian scarafaggio, Old Galician-Portuguese escaraveo), from Latin scarabaeus (“scarab, beetle”), from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “crab, beetle”). Cognate with English sc
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excarmināre, from Latin ex- + carminō (“to card”), from carmen (“card for wool, flax”). Compare Romanian scărmăna.
Apocope of escarnimiento, from Old Spanish escarnir (“to mock”), from Vulgar Latin *scarniō, from a hypothetical Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌽𐌾𐌰𐌽 (*skairnjan).

parole.significato: scarce, limited, scant, meager, meagre, skimpy, rare, insufficient, slight, slim
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *escarpsus, from Late Latin excarpsus (“rare”), from *excarpere (“pluck out”), from classical Latin excerpere. Related to English scarce.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excomborāre, of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *comboros, derived from *kom- (“with”) + *bereti (“to bear”), similar to Dutch kommer (“concern, problems”).
Inherited from Old Spanish escriván, from Vulgar Latin *scrībānem, from alteration of declension from Latin scrība (“writer, scribe”). Doublet of escriba, a borrowing.

parole.significato: to write (to form letters, words or symbols on a surface in order to communicate)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish escrivir, from Vulgar Latin *scrībīre, from Latin scrībere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exquadrāre.

From the older form escrudiñar, a semi-learned derivation from Vulgar Latin *scrūtiniāre, from Late Latin scrūtinium (“investigation, scrutiny”), from Latin scrūtārī (“to investigate, to scrutinize”).

parole.significato: to accompany someone out to say goodbye
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish escurrir, from Vulgar Latin *excorrigere, cognate with Italian scorgere (“to see, notice; guide, escort”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scalamus, from scalmus, from Ancient Greek σκαλμός (skalmós, “pin, thole”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, ultimately from Latin fortis (“strong”). Or, by surface analysis, es- + forzar.

Inherited from Old Spanish esfuerço, equivalent to a modern esforzar + -o. The Old Spanish etymon is similarly derived from esforçar, from a Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, from *fortiāre, from fortia (“heroic actions”). Compare Portuguese esforço, Catalan esforç, French effort, Italian sforzo. Cognate wi
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exmerāre (“to purify”).

From Vulgar Latin emorescĕre, frequentative of Latin ēmori, ēmorior (“to die (out)”), from Latin morior (“to die”), whence Spanish murrir (“to die”); but note also Old English smorian (“to choke, suffocate”). Cognate to Galician esmorecer and Portuguese esmorecer.

Inherited from Old Spanish espalda, from metathesis of Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spatula (“broad, flat piece”) (compare Catalan espatlla (“shoulder”), French épaule (“shoulder”), Portuguese espádua (“scapula, shoulder”)), diminutive of Latin spatha (“straight sword”). Doublet of espátula

parole.significato: to scare, to spook, to frighten
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Portuguese and Catalan espantar, Italian spaventare, French épouvanter, also Romanian înspăimânta.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stabiliscere, from Latin stabilīre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extorcere.
Inherited from Old Spanish estragar, from Vulgar Latin *stragāre, from Latin strāges (“defeat, slaughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- whence English strew and destroy.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stricāre or Latin extricāre. Compare Sicilian stricari, Old Italian stricare, strigare; cf. also Romanian strica. Cognate with English extricate.

Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], probably from a Vulgar Latin *extronĭtus, from *tronĭtus, from metathesis of Latin tonitrus. Compare Portuguese estrondo. Doublet of tronido, which came from a variant with stress on the penultimate syllable (long -i-).

parole.significato: to press, squeeze (so that liquid comes out)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extroculāre, derived (with metathesis of /r/) from Latin torculum (“wine or olive press”).
Inherited from Old Spanish fallesçer, derived from fallir (“to err, to fail”), from Vulgar Latin *fallīre (“to fail”), from Latin fallere (“to deceive”). Compare Portuguese falecer.
Inherited from Old Spanish fallir, inherited from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere. With irregular preservation of /f-/.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fallita, from the feminine of *fallitus, 'vulgar' past participle of Latin fallere. The preservation of initial /f/ is irregular, but Coromines & Pascual reject the possibility of the word being borrowed. Compare Portuguese falta, Catalan falta, French faute.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fīlī ecclēsiae (literally “son of the church”), from the vocative of Latin fīlius (“son”), and the genitive of ecclēsia (“church”). Cognate with Galician fregués and Portuguese freguês.
Inherited from Old Spanish fiar, from Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere with a change in conjugation.
Inherited from Old Spanish ficar (also fincar), from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of hincar.

Inherited from Old Spanish firme, inherited from Vulgar Latin *fīrmis, from Latin firmus, from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”). The preservation of initial /f/ is irregular, but Coromines & Pascual reject the possibility of the

Related to fuego, and possibly ultimately from a Vulgar Latin *focone, from focus, perhaps through Catalan fogó or through a Mozarabic intermediary, as it was attested relatively late and preserved the initial -f- as opposed to -h- (compare hogar, hoguera, hogaza, etc.). Cognate with Sicilian fucuni
From Old Spanish forçar, from Vulgar Latin *fortiāre, from Late Latin fortia, from Latin fortis.

Inherited from Old Spanish fragua, from older frauga, from a presumed earlier form *fravga, from a Vulgar Latin *frabica, a metathetic form of Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“forger, smith”). Doublet of froga, fábrica, and forja, the second borrowed from Latin and the third from French. Com
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *friscum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frictiāre, a frequentative based ultimately on Latin fricāre (through its past participle frĭctus).
From Vulgar Latin *frictiāre, from Latin fricare. Doublet of frezar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frīctūra. By surface analysis, fritar + -ura. Compare Portuguese fritura, French friture, Italian frittura, Romanian friptură.
From Vulgar Latin *focīlis [petra], derived from Latin focus.

parole.significato: a naturally occurring segment or piece of a fruit
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *galleus (“oaken”), from Latin galla (“oak apple”).
Inherited from Old Spanish gamo, from Vulgar Latin gammus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *camocia, from Late Latin camōx, from Gaulish camox, probably from an extinct Alpine language (Raetic, Ancient Ligurian), possibly Proto-Indo-European *kem- (“without horns”). Doublet of chamuz.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carpiniāre, from carpō.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carylium, *carulium, diminutive of Latin caryon, from Ancient Greek κάρυον (káruon, “nut”). Cognate with Italian gheriglio. Doublet of carozo, which was inherited via a different development.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, colphus, culfus, alteration of colpus following hypercorrection of the popular pronunciation of Latin 'ph' as 'p', itself from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos).

parole.significato: ruff (circular frill or ruffle on a garment)
parole.testo: From gorga + -era, from Vulgar Latin *gurga, from gurges.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *graclu(s), syncopated form of Latin grāculus (“jackdaw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *greh₂-k- (“croak”). Compare English grackle, Italian gracchio, and Portuguese gralho.

parole.significato: fat or grease used in cooking
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin grassa, from Latin crassus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin (Iberian dialect) *gracināre, related to Late Latin gracitāre and gracillāre, from the same imitative/onomatopoetic root as Latin graculus (“jackdaw”).
Inherited from Old Spanish crieta, from Vulgar Latin *crepta, from Latin crepita, passive participle of crepō (“to crack”).

parole.significato: to shout, to scream, to cry out, to call out
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *werrizāre. Derivable from guerra (“war”) + -ear (verb-forming suffix).
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *(petra) aquilea (“acute stone”), from aquileus (“acute”), from Latin aculeus.

parole.significato: a kind of torch or large candle (often with four sticks)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish facha, from a Vulgar Latin *fascla, from syncopation of *fascula, presumably from a crossing of Latin facula and fascis. Doublet of fácula, a borrowing. Cognate with Old Galician-Portuguese facha.
From earlier fada, from Vulgar Latin *Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Catalan fada, Occitan fada, Portuguese fada, French fée, Italian fata.

parole.significato: to find something, deliberately or not
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish fallar (“to find”), following internal consonant spread and palatalization, namely via Vulgar Latin *faflāre, from Latin afflāre (“to breathe or blow upon”). Cognate to Portuguese achar, Romanian afla. For the phonetic development, compare Old Spanish finchar, Spanish hinc

By surface analysis, hallar + -azgo. Inherited from Old Spanish falladgo (13th c.), maybe from an unattested Vulgar Latin *afflāticum, from Latin afflō. Cognate with Galician and Portuguese achádego, Leonese chalga and Asturian ayalga.

Inherited from Old Spanish fambre, fanbre, famne (whence also Ladino ambre), from Vulgar Latin *faminem (the accusative of a nominative *famen or *famis), variant of Latin famēs, see there for more. For other examples of Latin /mVn/ > Old Spanish /mn/ > /mɾ/ > /mbɾ/ see hombre, nombre, muchedumbre,
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *faminentus, from Latin famēs. Cognate with Galician famento and Portuguese faminto.

parole.significato: the hopper or drawer where grounded flour falls into
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *farināle, from Latin farīna.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fastigiāle, from Latin fastigium.
From earlier haedo, inherited from Vulgar Latin *fāgētum, from Latin fāgus. Influenced by haya. Compare Asturian fayéu, Italian faggeto, Romanian făget.
Inherited from Old Spanish feviella~fiviella (with /e/ < /i/ perhaps via dissimilation), from Vulgar Latin *fībella, diminutive of Latin fībula. Compare Portuguese fivela, Galician fibela.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fētibundus, from Latin fēteō, foeteō (“to have a bad smell, stink”). Compare the similar structured sabiondo.

Inherited from Old Spanish fenchir, enchir, from Vulgar Latin *implīre, from Latin implēre. More information According to Coromines & Pascual, the initial f- in Old Spanish was likely due to phonetic and semantic similarities with finchar > modern hinchar. In dwindling use by the 16th century, hench

parole.significato: small groove, slit or other indentation
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *findicula, from Latin findō (“to cleave, to split, to divide”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin ferrāmenta, from the plural of Latin ferrāmentum.
Inherited from Old Spanish fiel, from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.

From earlier fincar, from Old Spanish fincar, from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of ficar. The /n/ may be due to the influence of Latin fingere and its derivatives.
Inherited from Old Spanish finojo, from Vulgar Latin *fenuclum, from Latin fēnuculum, from a diminutive of Latin fēnum.

parole.significato: a kneading table; a table in which dough is kneaded
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *finctōrium, from *finctum + -ōrium, from Latin fictum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin fīctus, variant of Latin fīxus, perfect passive participle of fīgō. Doublet of fijo. Compare Catalan fita and Portuguese fito.
Inherited from Old Spanish fogar, from Vulgar Latin focāris, from Latin focus. Compare Galician fogar, English foyer.

Inherited from Old Spanish foguera, from Vulgar Latin *focāria, a nominalization of Latin focārius (“of or relating to hearths”), from focus (“fire”) + -ārius. Compare Portuguese fogueira, Catalan foguera, Italian focaia, Romanian focar, English foyer.
From follar, from Vulgar Latin *fullāre, from Latin fullo (“fuller”).

parole.significato: the skin or membrane covering some fruits and seeds, such as grapes, beans, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *folliclu, from Latin folliculus, diminutive form of follis (“purse, sack”). Compare the borrowed doublet folículo. Cognate with Portuguese folhelho.
Inherited from Old Spanish follín, from Vulgar Latin *fullīginem (compare the attested follīginem), from Latin fūlīginem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂li-, from *dʰewh₂-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *formīcārium, from Latin formīca. Compare Portuguese formigueiro, Catalan formiguer, Italian formicaio, Romanian furnicar.

parole.significato: a meat pie made with pork loin, chorizo and hard-boiled eggs
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fornāceus, from Latin fornāx (“oven”).

From horno + -illo (diminutive suffix); possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Italian fornello, Catalan fornell, Galician Fornelos (toponym), Occitan fornèl, Sicilian furneddu.

parole.significato: to root, dig with the snout
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fodiāre, from Latin fodere (“to dig”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰod- (“to pierce, dig”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ŏva f sg (“roe”), from Latin ōva n pl (“eggs”). Doublet of huevo (“egg”), from the Latin singular ōvum. Compare Portuguese ova.
Inherited from Old Spanish hueuo, from Vulgar Latin *ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum, from Proto-Italic *ōw(j)om, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm, from *h₂éwis, possibly from *h₂ew-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fugītīcius, from Latin fugere (“flee”). By surface analysis, huido + -izo.

Inherited from Old Spanish fuir~foir, from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, fugiō, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with French fuir, Portuguese fugir, Galician fuxir, Asturian afuxir, Catalan fugir.
Inherited from Old Spanish fumeyar, inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūmizāre, from Latin fūmigāre. Derivable from humo + -ear. Doublet of fumigar, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin forāneus (influenced in Spanish by hurón), ultimately from Latin forās (“outside”). Doublet of foráneo.
From Old Spanish furgar, from Vulgar Latin *fūricāre, from Latin fūr (“thief”) whence English ferret and furtive.
Inherited from Old Spanish eglesia (9th century), a semi-learned descendant of Vulgar Latin eclesia, from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “assembly”).

parole.significato: synonym of ijar, side (region between the ribcage and the hip)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *īliāta, from Latin īlia, plural of īle (“guts, intestines”). Compare English ilium.

parole.significato: flank, side, region between the ribcage and the hip in mammals
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *īliāris, from Latin īlia, plural of īle (“guts, intestines”). Cognate with English ileum, Portuguese ilhal and ilharga.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *antecordium (literally “tumor in the chest of horses”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin īnfantiō.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin insomnium. Doublet of ensueño.

parole.significato: island (area of land surrounded by water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish isla, from Vulgar Latin *īsula, from Latin īnsula (compare Catalan illa, French île, Galician insua, Italian isola, Portuguese ínsua). Doublet of ínsula, a borrowing. Cognate with English isle but false cognate of English island.
From ijadear, from ijada, from Vulgar Latin *iliata, from Latin īlia (“intestines, guts”). Compare English jade (“to tire, become fatigued”).
From Vulgar Latin *salma, from Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma).
Supposedly from the apheresis of Vulgar Latin pecuniola, from Latin pecūnia.

From Vulgar Latin *iuxtāre, from Latin iuxtā (“near, beside”). Probably arrived through the intermediate of Old Occitan jostar (and later influenced by justo) or Catalan justar. As it was a term relating to chivalry and knighthood, it may have been treated or seen as foreign, or it may have been inf
Inherited from Old Spanish lagarto, from Vulgar Latin *lacartum, from Latin lacertus.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin lacusta, from Latin locusta, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: to water up; to cry easily
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lacrimizāre. Synchronically lágrima (“teardrop”) + -ear (verb-forming suffix).
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *lumbrīc(u)la, from Latin lumbrīcus + -ula.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lamprēda (attested as Medieval Latin lampreda), of uncertain origin: possibly from Late Latin lampetra, from a combination of Latin lambō (“to lick”) and petra (“stone”). Compare Italian lampreda, French lamproie and Portuguese lampreia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *landa, from Gaulish *landā, from Proto-Celtic *landā.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glandinem (“acorn”), from Latin glāns.
Inherited from Old Spanish langosta, from Vulgar Latin lacusta, from Latin locusta.

From Vulgar Latin *lotōnem, derived from Latin lotus, a borrowing from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós). Coromines & Pascual posit that the Spanish word's unvoiced /-t-/ is due to borrowing from Aragonese, presumably meaning the Pyrenean varieties that did not lenite intervocalic Latin /p t k/.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus (“noose, trap”). Cognate with English lace.

Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *lenticla, from syncopation of Latin lenticula (compare French lentille, Italian lenticchia, Portuguese lentilha), diminutive form of lēns, lentis (“lentil”). Doublet of lentilla.
From leudo, from Vulgar Latin *levĭtus, as an alternative of Latin levātus. Compare Portuguese levedar, Italian lievitare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *levĭtum (“yeast, sourdough”), from Latin levātus (“lifted”). Compare Portuguese lêvedo and Asturian lleldu.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *levātīcius, from Latin levāre. By surface analysis, levado + -izo.
From lesna, from alesna, from Vulgar Latin *alisna, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *alasnō; cf. *ēlō, whence English awl. Compare also Catalan alena, French alêne, Italian lesina.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *limācea, from Latin limax (“slug”). Compare limaco.

Inherited from Old Spanish limosna, from older almosna, elemosina, from Vulgar Latin *alēmosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna (“alms”) (compare French aumône, Italian elemosina, Portuguese esmola), from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “pity, mercy”), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “pitiful, merciful”).
From the Romance/Vulgar Latin *līssius, from Ancient Greek λισσός (lissós, “smooth”). Compare Portuguese liso, French lisse, Catalan llis, Italian liscio.
From a Vulgar Latin *leviānus, from Latin levis. Compare Galician livián and Old Galician-Portuguese livão.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *flammizāre, from Latin flamma. Derivable from llama (“flame”) + -ear (verb-forming suffix). Cf. the doublets flamear and flambear.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plovere, from Classical Latin pluere. Compare Portuguese chover.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lumbrīcem, from Classical Latin lumbrīcus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *luscidus, from Latin luscus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūcīre, from Latin lūcēre.
Inherited from Old Spanish maslo, itself from Vulgar Latin masclus, contracted form of Latin masculus (“male”). Doublet of másculo.

Inherited from Old Spanish maçiço (mid-14th c.), from a hypothetical earlier *massizo, from Vulgar Latin *massīcius, from Latin massa (“mass”), from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “barley cake”); see links for more. The sense “massif” is a semantic loan from French massif, which is cognate.
From Old Spanish madrugar, madurgar, from Vulgar Latin *mātūricāre, derived from Latin maturāre (“hurry”) (whence Spanish madurar).
From an Iberian Vulgar Latin *mac(u)lāta, from Latin macula. Compare Portuguese malhada and Aragonese mallata.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mancipius (“slave”), from Latin mancipium (“purchase property”), also "a bought slave".
Likely from Vulgar Latin *manicella (with a change in suffix to -era), diminutive of Latin manicula, whence Spanish manija (“handle”). In any event, ultimately from Latin manus (“hand”).
Inherited from Old Spanish mancha, from Vulgar Latin *mancla, from Latin macula. Compare with the borrowed doublet mácula, as well as with mangla.

parole.significato: to spot, stain, mark, to smudge
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manclāre, maclāre, from Latin maculāre (“to stain”). Doublet of magular and macular.

parole.significato: stain; blemish (moral defect; a character flaw)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish manziella, from Vulgar Latin mancella, from Latin macella.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manizāre. Derivable from mano (“hand”) + -ear (verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Old Spanish manera (“manner”), from Vulgar Latin *man(u)āria, from the feminine of Latin manuārius. Compare Catalan manera, French manière, English manner & Portuguese maneira.

According to Corominas-Pascual, inherited from Old Spanish manganilla (c. 1300), from Vulgar Latin *manganella, plural of *manganellum, from Latin manganum (“mangonel”) + -ellus. Less likely, according to RAE, from mangana (“lasso”), which is instead considered by Corominas-Pascual to be a back-form
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mānsus, from Latin mānsuētus.

From earlier mazana, from Vulgar Latin *mattiāna, ellipsis of māla mattiāna, plural of Latin mālum mattiānum (literally “apple of Matius”), referring to a kind of apple. Gaius Matius, a friend of Julius Caesar and Cicero, was a Roman horticulturist and author of cookbooks. Cognate with Portuguese ma

Likely from the Vulgar Latin māreposā, which is a combination of māra (meaning "to flutter") and *pōsa (suggesting "to rest"). Another theory suggests it comes from the phrase María pósate (“Mary, alight!”). This likely stems from the belief that butterflies were the souls of the dead, and the Virgi
Two sources are presented: * From Vulgar Latin marecadicus. Related to French marécage. * From Arabic مرج (marj, “meadow”). Probably both through Catalan marjal.

From a Vulgar Latin *ma(t)tea, from Latin mateola, from a Proto-Indo-European root describing similar tools; see also Old High German medela (“plow”), Old Church Slavonic мотыка (motyka, “mattock”), Sanskrit मत्य (matya, “club, harrow”). Related to Portuguese maça, Catalan maça, French masse, Italia
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mania (“manual skill”), from Latin manus (“hand”). The sense of "mania" may have been influenced by manía, from the (unrelated) Latin mania. Compare Portuguese manha.
Inherited from Old Spanish mannana (literally “tomorrow morning”), from Vulgar Latin *māneāna, from Latin māne, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂-. Compare Portuguese manhã.
From Old Spanish medroso, from Vulgar Latin *metōrōsum, derived from Latin metus (“fear”, noun).
From earlier mexilla, maxiella, from Vulgar Latin *maxella, from Latin maxilla.

parole.significato: born during the same birthing, especially from a double birthing
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish emelgo, emielgo, from Vulgar Latin *gemellicum, from Latin gemellus, from geminus "twin, paired", (compare French jumeau, Italian gemello, Portuguese gêmeo, Romanian geamăn). See mielgo.
Uncertain; possibly of pre-Roman origin, or perhaps from Vulgar Latin *gemellō, *gemellāre, from Latin gemellus (cf. mellizo). See also the related mella.

parole.significato: twin (fraternal, born to the same parents at the same time)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish emellizo, from Vulgar Latin *gemellīcius, from Latin gemellus.

parole.significato: stale bread; breadcrust (particularly the heel of a loaf)
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *mandūcum, from Latin mandūcāre. Influenced by mendigo (“beggar”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *merēscere, from Latin merēre.

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin minimāre, a verb based on Latin minimus (“least”). Considering its rather late date of first attestation in Spanish (1603) and the absence of an inherited Portuguese counterpart, Coromines & Pascual suppose it was likely borrowed, through mercantile contacts, from Occita

parole.significato: to pull out; to tear out (hair)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *messāre, from Latin metĕre (“to harvest, reap, cut off”).
From Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāta, from Latin mānsiō.
Inherited from Old Spanish miel, myel, from Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin melica, from Latin medica (“Median”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gemellicum, from Latin gemellus, diminutive of geminus. Compare Galician xemelgo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mīcācula, diminutive from Latin mīca (“crumb”). Synchronically miga + -aja.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *milānus, from milvinus, from Latin milvus.

parole.significato: same; identical; one and the same; indicates that the two compared noun clauses both represent the one thing
parole.testo: From earlier mesmo, from Old Spanish mesmo and the rare medesmo (1259, in a Carta de orden), from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus (compare French même, Italian medesimo, Portuguese mesmo), from Latin -met, an emphatic suffix, + ipsimus (“the very same”).
From moco + -oso, possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin *muccōsus < Late Latin mūcōsus, from Latin mūcus. Doublet of mucoso.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“soak”), a verb based on Latin mollis (“soft”). Compare Catalan mullar, Portuguese molhar, French mouiller.
From Hispanic Vulgar Latin *mūtulōnem, from Latin mūtulus. Compare French moellon, Italian modiglione.

Uncertain: * from Vulgar Latin *mōmus, from Ancient Greek Μῶμος (Mômos, “god of satire and mockery”), from μῶμος (mômos); * from an imitative Proto-Germanic root, whence Dutch mom (“mask”), German Mumme (“mask”) - see mummer. * from Old French momer (“to wear a mask”), related to momon (“mask”), fro
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mōra, from Latin mōrum (whose plural was reanalyzed as the feminine singular), probably Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
From Vulgar Latin *mordacia, from Latin mordax. Compare Portuguese mordaça, French mordache, Italian mordacchia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *murrum, *morrum (“mound, hillock”), cognate with Occitan morre.

parole.significato: Sorbus spp., especially common whitebeam (Aria edulis, syn. Sorbus aria)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin extension of Latin mustum (“must”), because of the berries being stored in must or tasting of wine. See Arabic مُشْتَهَى (muštahā) for cognates. Doublet of mostellar from Leonese mostellar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *movitīcius, from Latin movēre (“move”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *multificāre (“multiply, increase”), from Latin multus (“much”) + -ficāre (factitive verb-forming suffix).
From a Proto-Romance/Vulgar Latin root *mocc-, imitative of laughter. See also Middle French moquer, Portuguese moca, English mock.

Inherited from Old Spanish muerto (“dead”), from Vulgar Latin *mortu(s), from Latin mortuus. Cognate with Bengali মৃত (mrito) / মৃত্যু (mrittu), Hindi मृत (mŕt) / मृत्यु (mŕtyu), Russian мёртвый (mjórtvyj), смерть (smertʹ).
Deverbal from moscar, from Vulgar Latin *mossicāre, from Latin morsicāre (“to nibble, to chew”).

parole.significato: bat (any flying mammal of the order Chiroptera)
parole.testo: Metathetic form of earlier murciégalo, a diminutive of Old Spanish murciego, from Vulgar Latin *mūrem caecum (literally “blind mouse”). Compare Galician and Portuguese morcego.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *morrum, *murrum (“hillock, mound, snout”), in the sense of frowning or puckered lips. Cognate with Italian mogio.

parole.significato: thigh (upper leg of a human, between the hip and the knee)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *mūsclus, from Latin mūsculus (“muscle”). Doublet of the borrowed músculo.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *mustidus, from mustum (“must”) + -idus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nārīcūtus, ultimately derived from Latin nāris. By surface analysis, nariz + -udo.
Cognate with French narine and Portuguese narina, from Vulgar Latin *narīna, from Latin nāris (“nostril”), from nāsus (“nose”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *navācla, from Latin novācula (“razor”), from Proto-Italic *(ks)nowātlā. Compare Portuguese navalha, Galician navalla, Asturian navaya.
Inherited from Old Spanish nevar, from Vulgar Latin *nevāre, ultimately from Latin nivem (“snow”, noun).
Inherited from Old Spanish nieve, from Vulgar Latin *nĕvem, alteration of Latin nivem.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ninnus, probably imitative of infantile language; also could have originated from Latin minimus. Compare also Italian nino and Sicilian nicu. Compare English nun for an English word that is formed similarly from imitative origin of infantile speech, as well as possibly n
Inherited from Old Spanish novaenta, from Vulgar Latin *nōvāgintā, from Latin nōnāgintā (blended with novem (“nine”)), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *novius (“newlywed”), related to Latin novus (“new”). Compare with the Portuguese noivo, Catalan nuvi.

parole.significato: knot (a looping piece of a long, flexible material)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *nūdus, from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”). Compare to Portuguese nó. Doublet of nodo. Also compare English noose.
Inherited from Old Spanish nuera, from Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nŏcem, alteration of Latin nucem (from which the expected outcome would have been *noz).

From Vulgar Latin *nutria or *lutria / *lutrea, from Latin lutra. The Spanish word, preserving the -t-, may have arrived through the intermediate of either Mozarabic or more likely a Southern Italian language or dialect: cf. Salerno dialect (of Neapolitan) nùtria, Calabrian ùtria and lùtria, utre in

Inherited from Old Spanish niéspero, néspero, from Vulgar Latin *nespirum, from Latin mespilum, borrowed from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon), most likely of non-Indo-European origin. For the development of the stressed vowel, compare avispa (from Old Spanish biespa) and víspera (from Old Spanish

parole.significato: to offer, to offer up, to provide
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ofresçer, derived from ofrir, from Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.
Inherited from Old Spanish ojo, from Vulgar Latin oclus, from Classical Latin oculus. Doublet of óculo. Cognate to Portuguese olho, French œil, Italian occhio, Romanian ochi. Compare English ogle.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *olīvus, from Latin olīva, olīvum.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin olor, from Latin odor, influenced by oleō. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Cognate with English odor.
Inherited from Old Spanish olbidar, olvidar, from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, frequentative of Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *undizāre. Derivable from onda + -ear.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aurizāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aurīna, alteration of Latin ūrīna.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ōrula, diminutive of Latin ōra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ōrulāre, from *ōrula, diminutive of Latin ōra. Compare Italian orlare, French ourler.

parole.significato: any of several species of fungus of the genus Amanita
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *auruncula (compare French oronge (“agaric”)).
Inherited from Old Spanish oruga, from Vulgar Latin urūca, from Latin ērūca (whence English arugula), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰer(s)-uk-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *aurīginem, from alteration of Latin aerūginem (“copper rust”), with influence from aurum (“gold”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ossāmen (“bones”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *falvārium, from falvus, from Proto-Germanic *falwaz. Cognate with Portuguese fouveiro, Catalan falb, French fauve, and further German fahl, falb, English fallow. The expected Spanish spelling would be hovero, which is attested.
From ovillo + -ar, from Vulgar Latin globellus (possibly through a form *lobellus), diminutive of Latin globus. Cf. also Portuguese novelo.
From Old Spanish pavilo, from Vulgar Latin *papīlum, from Latin papȳrus. Doublet of papiro.
Inherited from Old Spanish padesçer, derived from padir, from Vulgar Latin *patīre, from Latin patī.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin patrastrum, derivative of Latin pater. By surface analysis, padre + -astro.

parole.significato: palate (roof of the mouth, and sense of taste)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *palātārem, derived from Latin palātum.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from the accusative form of Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “log, trunk, body of soldiers, etc.”). Cf. Italian palanca, English plank, planch, as well as Spanish plancha, an etymological doublet.
Inherited from Old Spanish paloma, from Vulgar Latin palumba, from Latin palumbus, palumbēs (“wood pigeon”).
From Vulgar Latin *papaverīna, from papāver (“poppy”). Doublet of papaverina.
From Vulgar Latin *pandurica, from Late Latin pandūra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin pānāria, from Latin pānārium, from pānis (“bread”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin pānucla < pānucula, from Latin pānicula, diminutive of pānus (“ear of millet”). Doublet of panícula.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre.

parole.significato: to pass, to hand, to slip
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish passar, from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun). Compare English pass.
From Vulgar Latin *pasmus, from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”). Compare English patten.

parole.significato: tall tale (a greatly exaggerated, fantastic story)
parole.testo: From earlier pastraña, from Vulgar Latin pastoranea, from Latin pastor.

parole.significato: spark (small glowing particle emanated from burning matter)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pulvisia, from Latin pulvis (“dust”).
From Vulgar Latin *pavōrōsum, derived from Latin pavōrem (“fear”, noun). By surface analysis, pavor + -oso.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *petīre, from Latin petere (“ask, request”). Compare English petition.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin peca, from Latin pīca (“magpie”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peyk- (“woodpecker; magpie”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vellicicāre, from Latin vellicāre, most likely ultimately from vellus (“the wool shorn from a sheep, fleece, or pelt”). Cognate with English vellicate.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pectinī̆culum, diminutive of Latin pecten (“pubic hair; comb”). The unexpected /nd/ may be due to the influence of pender (“hang down, dangle”). Compare Portuguese pentelho.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *peccuinnus, from *pittīnus, perhaps from a Celtic or Frankish root (cf. Proto-Celtic *biggos (“small”); Old Irish bec, Irish beag, Welsh bach/bychan, Breton bihan). Compare Portuguese pequeno, cf. also French petit.
Inherited from Old Spanish pera, from Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *peraltus (“very high”).
Inherited from Old Spanish permanesçer, from Vulgar Latin *permanēscere, from Latin permanēre.

parole.significato: to pursue, to chase, to go after
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish perseguir, from Vulgar Latin *persequīre, from Latin persequī. By surface analysis, per- + seguir. Cognate with English persecute.

parole.significato: weight (the force on an object due to gravitational attraction)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish peso, from Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum, from pendō (“to weigh”). Doublet of the semi-learned pienso.

From Old Spanish pestaña (“eyelash and eyebrow area; eyelash”), cognate with Portuguese pestana (“eyelash”), Catalan pestanya (“eyelash”) and Gascon Occitan pestana, from Vulgar Latin *pistanna, and related to Basque pizta (“rheum, eye sleep”) and piztule (“pestaña”). Coromines and Pascual conjectur
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pestellus, diminutive of Late Latin pestulus, alteration of Latin pessulus. Compare Catalan pestell.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *post auriculum, an alteration of the phrase post auriculam (literally “behind the ear”). The change of gender from feminine to masculine is unexplained.
From a Vulgar Latin *pecione, a derivative of Late Latin peciolus, petiolus, from *pediciolus, diminutive of Latin pedīculus, diminutive form of pēs (“foot”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīlāre, from Latin pīla (“pillar”).
Probably from Old Spanish *peltraza, from Vulgar Latin *pertrāctiāre (“to pull apart”), from Latin per- (“through”) + trahere (“to pull, drag”).
Most likely from a crossing of punchar (itself a variant of punzar, from Vulgar Latin *punctiāre, from Latin punctus), and picar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pinctāre < *pictāre, frequentative from Latin pingere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pinctus (“painted”), replacing Classical Latin pictus. Compare Sicilian pintu.
Inherited from Old Spanish pintor, from Vulgar Latin *pinctor, from Latin pictor, from pingō (“to paint, embroider”, supine stem pict-) + -tor (“-er”).
Inherited from Old Spanish pintura, from Vulgar Latin *pinctūra, from Latin pictūra, from pictus with influence from the present stem pingō.
From Vulgar Latin *pipa, from Latin pipō (“to pip”).

From Vulgar Latin *platta, *plattus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide”), because silver was often made into sheets. As with plato, this word may be semi-learned or avoided certain phonetic changes due to use by mainly the upper classes. Compare Portuguese prata, Catalan plata. Displ

From Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús); this Spanish word may be semi-learned or else one that was used primarily by the upper classes in the Middle Ages (in contrast to the lower classes, who did not often use plates to eat), and hence retained a more learned character close

parole.significato: either of two closely related trees:
parole.testo: Irregularly from Vulgar Latin *plōppus, from classical Latin pōpulus. Doublet of chopo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pulverēta, collective of *pulvus, pulveres, from Latin pulvis (“powder, dust”). Compare Catalan polseguera.

parole.significato: dust (fine, dry particles of matter found in the air and covering the surface of objects)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish polvos (singular), from Vulgar Latin *pulvus, neuter form derived from Classical Latin pulvis m, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Compare English pulverise.

parole.significato: stern, poop (back of a boat or ship)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish popa, from Vulgar Latin *puppa, from Latin puppis (“stern”), possibly with influence from prora (“prow”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pustella, from Latin pustula. Compare Portuguese bostela, Galician bostela, Asturian postiella.
From Vulgar Latin *postrārius, from Latin postrēmus, with + -ārius by analogy with prīmārius. Compare Portuguese postreiro.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pulliter, from Latin pullus (“young animal”). Cognate with Italian poltro (“untamed, lazy”).
Inherited from Old Spanish preguntar, from Vulgar Latin *praecūnctāre, alteration of Latin percontārī.
From Vulgar Latin prēnsus, from Latin prehēnsus.
Metathesis of older petril, from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *pectōrīlis, *pectōrīle, from Latin pectus (“chest”). Compare Portuguese peitoril.

Inherited from Old Spanish petrina, from Vulgar Latin *pectorīna, substantivized from the feminine of an adjective *pectorīnus, from Latin pectus (“chest”) + -īnus (adjectival suffix). Compare pretal, pretil, apretar.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin praegnāre (attested in Medieval Latin), back-formed from Latin praegnāns (“pregnant”), from earlier praegnās, formed from prae- (“before”) and the root of nāscor (“to be born”).

parole.significato: dark, swarthy (used to describe both people and landscapes)
parole.testo: From apretar (“squeeze, constrict, compress”). The semantic evolution to "dark" comes through the sense of "dense" or "thick". Another common, but less likely, etymology suggested is Vulgar Latin *prettus, from Latin pressus. Compare Portuguese preto, Asturian prietu.

parole.significato: to drench, dip, or coat in grease or fat
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, from Latin pendō (“to hang”). Compare possible cognate Asturian pingar.

parole.significato: bow, prow (front of a boat or ship)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish proda, from Vulgar Latin *prōda, from Latin prōra (via dissimilation), borrowed from Ancient Greek πρῷρα (prōîra), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-, form of *por-. Compare Italian proda.
From Vulgar Latin *prōgenitūra, from Latin prōgignō (“to beget”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *prōmissa (“promise”) (attested in Medieval Latin per Du Cange), from Latin prōmissum (“promise”), from promittō (“to send forth; to promise”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pūtīre, from Latin pūtēre.
From the older podrir, from Vulgar Latin *putrīre, from Latin putrēre; compare English putrid.
From Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post. Compare English post-, Old Galician-Portuguese pós, Italian poi, Romanian păi, apoi.

parole.significato: flea (a small, wingless, parasitic insect of the order Siphonaptera, renowned for its bloodsucking habits and jumping a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish pulga, from Vulgar Latin *pūlica, from Latin pūlex (whence English puce), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plus-.

parole.significato: English or American inch (a unit of length equal to 2.54 cm)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pollicāta, unit of length derived from Latin pollex (“thumb”). Compare Galician pulgada (which may be borrowed from Spanish) or Portuguese polegada. As an English unit, a calque of English inch.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pūlicōnem, from Latin pūlicem (“flea”). Compare Portuguese pulgão, Catalan pugó.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; nodo incerto nell'albero; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish puta, from a Vulgar Latin *pūtta, of uncertain origin, perhaps derived from Latin *puta, female form of Latin putus (“teeny boy”), a hapax legomenon of dubious reading. This etymology is supported by both María Moliner and Joan Coromines. Cognate with French pute, Catalan

parole.significato: sharp point on the tip of the vara (bullfighter's lance)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pūgia, from Latin pūgiō (“dagger”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pūgnāle(m), based on Latin pūgnus (“fist”).

Inherited from Old Spanish páxaro, pássaro, from Vulgar Latin *passarum, alteration of Latin passer (“sparrow”). Compare Portuguese pássaro, Dalmatian paserain, French passereau. A distant cognate of peña.
From Vulgar Latin *palpetrum, from Latin palpebra.

From Vulgar Latin *perdita, from the feminine of Latin perditus. Coromines & Pascual regard it as a semi-learned rather than popular form. Romance cognates include Portuguese perda, Italian perdita, French perte.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pugia, from Latin pungō (“to prick, to puncture, to sting”). Cognate with Galician puga, púa, Catalan pua, Portuguese pua.
From Old Spanish quebrantar, crebantar, from Vulgar Latin *crepantāre, derived from Latin crepere (“rattle”).

parole.significato: to be (as a result of something), to end up
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish quedar, from Vulgar Latin *quētāre, from Late Latin quiētō, -āre. Doublet of learned quietar and semi-learned quitar. Cognate with English quit and quiet.

parole.significato: to complain, to whine, to gripe, to grouse, to fuss, to bitch, to beef
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quassiare, from Latin quassāre. Doublet of cascar. Cognate with English quash.
Inherited from Old Spanish quemar, from Vulgar Latin *caimāre, a Greek-influenced modification of Latin cremāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *caria, from Latin cariēs (“decay”).

Inherited from Old Spanish quexada (cf. also quexar), from a Vulgar Latin *capseāta, derivative of *capseus (“chin”), itself a derivative of Latin capsa (“box”). Compare Portuguese and Galician queixada and queixo.
Inherited from Old Spanish quiçab, from qui sabe (“who knows”), ultimately from the Vulgar Latin expression qui sapit (“who knows”). Compare Italian chissà, Portuguese quiçá, and Catalan quissà.
From Vulgar Latin *rādīcōnem, augmentative form of rādīx (“root”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rāsāre. Compare English raze. Attested 1495.
Inherited from Old Spanish rascar, from Vulgar Latin *rāsicāre, a frequentative verb based on Latin rāsus (“shaven”).

parole.significato: to file down or sand down
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *raspāre, from Frankish *hraspōn.

From earlier restojo, from Vulgar Latin *restuclu < *restucŭlum (compare Portuguese restolho, Aragonese restollo, Catalan rostoll, restoll, Occitan restolh, cf. also southern Italian dialectal restuccio), variant of *restupŭlum (compare Catalan restoble, Occitan restoble), from a verb *restupulāre,

parole.significato: rat (medium-sized rodent belonging to the Rattus genus)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin rattus (“rat”), of Germanic origin. It is not known how the noun made the jump to a feminine noun.
Inherited from Old Spanish raça, from Vulgar Latin *radia, from Latin radius. Probably a doublet of raya. Compare also Romanian rază (“ray of light”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rapīnāre, from Latin rapīna (“plunder, rapine”), and thus from the same source as English rapine.

parole.significato: to back up, to go back, to step back, to move backward, to shrink back
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *revirāre, from re- + *virāre (whence possibly virar), probably a variation of Latin vibrāre or gȳrāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rebūcināre, from Latin re- + būcinō (“to sound a trumpet”), from būcina (“bugle, war trumpet”).

parole.significato: to gather; to safeguard; to collect
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *recapitāre. Doublet of recaudar and recadar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *recapitāre. Doublet of recaudar and recabdar.
Deverbal from recadar, from Vulgar Latin *recapitō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *recalceāre. By surface analysis, re- + calzar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *recaptāre, from Latin re- + captāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *recapitāre. Compare Portuguese arrecadar. Doublet of recadar and recabdar.
Inherited from Old Spanish rezio, probably from a Vulgar Latin *recidus, *ricidus, alteration of Latin rigidus. If so, a doublet of rígido.

parole.significato: to twist hard; to spin too much
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *refilare, which is derived from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *refūsāre, a blend of Latin refūtāre and recūsāre.

parole.significato: plowshare (or ploughshare) (soil-cutting bar of a plough)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *regla, from Latin rēgula (“bar, stick; rule, model”). Doublet of regla. Cognate with English rail.
From Vulgar Latin *rehinnitulāre, from Latin hinnitŭlus or hinnītus, perfect passive participle of hinniō (“to neigh”). Cognate of Galician rinchar.
From Vulgar Latin *remanescere, from Latin remaneō (“to remain”).
From Vulgar Latin *rememorāre, from Classical Latin rememorāri.
From Vulgar Latin *remurclāre, *remulculāre < remulcāre, from Latin remulcum (“towrope”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ringella, from ringī (whence reñir).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rēnicus, from Latin rēn.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *repositārius, from Latin repositus; cf. repositorius.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *repostus, from Classical Latin repositus.

parole.significato: to stick out; to jut out
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *resalīre. By surface analysis, re- + salir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *reexcaptāre, from Latin captāre. Compare English rechase and recatch.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *resufflāre, from re- + Latin sufflāre.

parole.significato: the opening between the door and doorjamb
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish rescrieço, Vulgar Latin *excrepitiare, from crepitiare, crepō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *restuculu(m), a variant of *restupulu(m) from Latin stupula, a variant of stipula (“stalk, stubble”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *resoltus, from Latin resolūtus. Doublet of resoluto.
From retortijar + -ón, from re- + Vulgar Latin *tortiliāre, from Latin tortilis (“twisted, coiled”). Cf. French tortiller, Italian tortiglione.

parole.significato: to go back, to back up
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *retractare, from Latin retractus, past participle of retraho.

parole.significato: to burst, explode, blow up, break
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *repentare, akin to repentino (“sudden”) and de repente (“suddenly”).
Inherited from Old Spanish rebuelto, from Vulgar Latin *revoltus, from Latin revolūtus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rīdīre (with dissimilation?), from Latin rīdēre. The perfect system and past participle were changed; the expected preterite indicative would be *rese or *rise with the expected past participle being *reso or *riso.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ringīre, from Latin ringī.

parole.significato: risk; the possibility of harm or an unfavorable outcome from random chance
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish riesco, possibly from Vulgar Latin *resecum, deverbal of Latin resecō. Doublet of risco.

parole.significato: to injure the hips or loin
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *renicāre, derived from *renio (“kidney”).
Deverbal from riscar or inherited from Vulgar Latin *resecum.
Latin risus + -eño. Probably from Vulgar Latin *risoneum, *risoneus. Cognate with Galician risoño. Portuguese risonho.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rīvāria, from Latin rīvus (“brook, small stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós, from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move, set in motion”) + *-wós.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rēniōnem, from Latin rēn (“kidney”). Cognate with Italian rognone and French rognon. Compare the more archaic word rene.

parole.significato: roan (having a coat of a dark base color with individual white hairs mixed in)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *ravidānus, from Latin ravĭdus, formed from rāvus (“grey, tawny”). Or, from Old Spanish roudano, a Germanic borrowing, from Gothic 𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌰𐌹 (raudai), inflection of 𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌸𐍃 (rauþs, “red”).
Inherited from Old Spanish ruciar, from Vulgar Latin *rōscidāre, derived from Latin rōscidus. Compare Portuguese rociar, Catalan ruixar.

parole.significato: dew (moisture on cool surfaces that condenses from the surrounding moist air)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish rucio, or deverbal from rociar, from Vulgar Latin *rōscidare, from Latin rōscidus (“filled with dew”), from rōs (“dew”).

parole.significato: rhinitis, coryza (inflammation of the mucous membranes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *rheumaticium, an alteration of Latin rheumaticum, an inflection of rheumaticus. From Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “flow”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rōmārius, alteration of rōs maris, equivalent of Latin rōsmarīnus. Compare Catalan romer, French romarin and English rosemary.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rōsāta, derived from Latin rōs.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ruptiāre, from Latin ruptus (“broken”). Compare Portuguese roçar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sevandīlia, possibly of Basque origin. Compare Portuguese sevandija.
From Vulgar Latin *sapidibundus (“growing with wisdom, increasing knowledge”), from Late Latin sapidus (“wise”), from Latin sapiō (“to know”). Spelling by conflation with hondo (“deep”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin segusius (compare Portuguese sabujo, Italian segugio), from a Celtic language, from Proto-Celtic *segu (“to follow”) (compare Irish seach).

parole.significato: a kind of hoe or mattock
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sarclum, from Latin sarculum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *salāre, from a change in conjugation of Latin salīre (“to salt”), from sal. Cognate with Catalan salar, French saler, Italian salare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *salsa, noun use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), from saliō, from sal.
Uncertain, possibly from Vulgar Latin *sarica, from Latin serica, and thus a doublet of jerga. Cf. also French serge, Old French sarge, Old Occitan sarga.

parole.significato: dermatitis, rash (area of reddened, irritated, and inflamed skin)
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin serpŭcŭlus, from Latin sĕrpō (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sagia, from Latin sagum, from sagus, possibly borrowed from Gaulish *sagos, *sagom, from a Celtic language, from Proto-Indo-European *seg-. Compare Portuguese saia, French saie. Doublet of sayo.

Inherited from Old Spanish sayo, from Vulgar Latin *sagium, from Latin sagum, from sagus, possibly borrowed from Gaulish *sagos, *sagom, from a Celtic language, from Proto-Indo-European *seg-. Compare with Galician saio (“robe”). Doublet of saya (“skirt”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sequīre, from deponent Classical Latin sequī, sequor, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Cognate with English segue, suit, sequel, sequence, and sue.
From Vulgar Latin *similiantem, present participle of *similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, semejar + -ante. Compare Galician semellante, Portuguese semelhante.
From Vulgar Latin *similiāre, a verb derived from Latin similis (“similar”). Compare Portuguese semelhar. More or less a doublet of simular.

Inherited from Old Spanish senziello, from Vulgar Latin *singellus, from Latin singulus. Compare Portuguese singelo, Catalan senzill, Asturian cenciellu. See also sendos, which was inherited directly from Latin singulus.
Probably from an Old Spanish form *suerba, from Vulgar Latin *sorba, feminine singular formed from the plural of sorbum.
Vulgar Latin *senara, of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *senara (“piece of land cultivated on the side”), from *sen- (“separation”) (<< Proto-Indo-European *swé (“self”)) + *aryeti (“to plow”).
From Old Spanish sessegar, from Vulgar Latin *sessicāre, from Latin sessus (“seated”), participle form of sedeō (“to sit”).
Inherited from Old Spanish sennero, from Vulgar Latin *sing(u)lāriu(s), from Latin singulāris (“alone, singular”). Doublet of singular.

parole.significato: mister, sir, lord (title conferred on a married or older male)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish sennor (“lord”), from Vulgar Latin *senjor (“master, elder, lord, nobleman”), from Latin seniōrem (“elder”), comparative form of senex (“old”). Doublet of sénior, borrowed from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *superculum.
From a Vulgar Latin root *superānus or *superiānus, from Latin super. Compare French souverain, Italian sovrano, soprano, Portuguese soberano, Catalan sobirà. Doublet of soprano, from Italian.
Inherited from Old Spanish sofreir, from Vulgar Latin *subfrigere, *suffrigere, from Latin sub- + frigere. By surface analysis, so- + freír. Compare with Catalan sofregir, Italian soffriggere.

From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin sōca, of Celtic origin, from Gaulish *soukā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to bend, to cut, to drive”), see also Sanskrit सुवति (suvati). Compare Portuguese and Asturian soga, Italian soga, French suage, Friulian soe, Romansh suga, Venetan soga.

Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin suggluttium (attested in some glosses), ultimately from Latin singultus, influenced by gluttiō. Cognate of Portuguese soluço, Romanian sughiț; also related to French sanglot, Italian singhiozzo, from *singlutium. Doublet of singulto.

Inherited from Old Spanish soltar, from a Vulgar Latin *soltāre (a root), from *solutāre, as a frequentative of Latin solvere. Equivalent to suelto + -ar (with -ue- becoming -o- due to destressing of that syllable).

parole.significato: shadow (a dark image projected onto a surface where light (or other radiation) is blocked by the shade of an object)
parole.testo: Possibly from the verb sombrar (from Vulgar Latin *subumbrāre), or more likely from Latin umbra (“shade, shadow”), possibly altered by influence from sol (“sun”) (cf. Old Spanish solombra (literally “sunshade”)) or the Latin prefix sub-. An alternative explanation for this form is a Latin constructi
From Vulgar Latin *sonācula, plural of *sonāculum, from Latin sonāre (“to make noise”).

Inherited from Old Spanish sonreir, from Vulgar Latin *subrīdīre, from Latin subrīdēre. Compare Portuguese sorrir, Galician sorrir. Also compare the obsolete Old Spanish sonrisar. By surface analysis, son- + reír.

Unknown. Various theories exist: * From Vulgar Latin sopiō. * From a crossing between sopetón and *arreponcio. * From a Late Latin phrase sub Pontiō Pīlātō, which supposedly meant crucified under Pontius Pilate.
Inherited from Old Spanish sessegar, from Vulgar Latin *sessicāre, from Latin sessus, perfect passive participle of sedeō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūbella, from Latin sūbula (“shoemaker's awl”), from Proto-Indo-European *syuHdʰleh₂, from *syewH- (“sew”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sola, from Latin solea (“sole”). Compare Portuguese sola, Galician sola, Italian suola.
Inherited from Old Spanish suelto, from Vulgar Latin *soltus, from Latin solūtus, perfect passive participle of solvō (“to loosen”). Compare English solute. Doublet of soluto.

parole.significato: to suffer (be confronted with something undesired)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish sufrir, sofrir, from Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.
From a Vulgar Latin root *sūrtus < *sūrctus, from Latin surrēctus.

From alteration of Old Spanish sotalo, from Vulgar Latin *subtulus, diminutive of Latin subtus (“below”). Compare Portuguese sótão (“attic”). Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *subtānus (whence Italian sottano), itself also a derivative of subtus (“below”).

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *tacca, *tecca, of Germanic origin, from Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌺𐌽𐍃 (taikns, “mark, sign”), from Proto-Germanic *taiknaz, *taikniz (“sign, mark”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-. Influenced by forms related to Frankish *stakjan, *stakkjan and Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌺𐍃 (staks, “mark”). See attacher
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tālōnem, augmentative of tālus (“ankle; heel”). Compare Medieval Latin tālō. Cognate with English talon.

Together with Portuguese tamujo from Vulgar Latin, an ancient Berber borrowing. Occurs in Latin Tamugadis ~ Thamugadi, name of a town on the Eastern Algerian coast the ruins of which are now known as Timgad.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *taxitāre. Compare Italian tastare and French tâter.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *teglātu, from Latin tēgulātum, from tēgula (“a roof-tile”). Compare Portuguese telhado, Galician tellado, Catalan teulada.
From Vulgar Latin *tēlāria, from Latin tēlum (“dart”). Cognate with Galician tieira.
Probably deverbal from temperar. May correspond to a Vulgar Latin *temperium, from Latin temperiēs (compare Catalan temper, temperi, Occitan tempier, Old French tempier, Italian temperie).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *terrāceus, from Latin terra.
From a Vulgar Latin *tēnsāre, from Latin tēnsus, perfect passive participle of tendō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīnac(u)la, diminutive of Latin tīna. By surface analysis, tina + -aja.
From Vulgar Latin tinctāre; see Latin tīnctus (“dipped in; tinged”) for more.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tōfa, from Latin tōfus.
Inherited from Old Spanish touiello, from Vulgar Latin *tūbellum, a diminutive of Latin tūber (“hump, bump, swelling, protuberance”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *toccāre, *tuccāre, of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *tusculus, diminutive of Latin tuscus.
From dissimilation from toñina, from Vulgar Latin *thunnina, from Latin thunnus (“tuna”), alluding to the blows used to finish off this fish once its caught.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *thymellus, diminutive of Latin thymus, from Ancient Greek θύμος (thúmos).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *thunnina, from Latin thunnus (“tuna”), from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos). Compare Catalan tonyina.
Inherited from Old Spanish torbelino, following dissimilation from torbenino, from Vulgar Latin *turbinīnus, diminutive of Latin turbinem. Compare Catalan terbolí.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tauribundus, from Latin taurus (“bull”) + -bundus. By surface analysis, toro + -ondo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tornātīcius, from Latin tornāre. By surface analysis, tornado + -izo.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin tuscus (literally “Etruscan, Tuscan”), from Vicus Tuscus (“Etruscan neighbourhood”), the Etruscan quarter of Rome, whose dwellers had a reputation of being poor and unruly. See Vicus Tuscus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *thunnīna. Doublet of atún.
Inherited from Old Spanish trabajar, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), derived from Late Latin tripālium (“torture instrument”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *taranca (compare Old French taranche (“big iron pin”)), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *tarankyos (“nail”) (compare Middle Irish tairnge (“iron nail”)), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to drill, rub”).

Inherited from Old Spanish trasfegar, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcāre (from fricō (“to rub”)) or *trānsfaecāre (from faex (“dregs”)). Cognate with Portuguese and Galician trasfegar, Catalan trafegar, Italian trafficare.

parole.significato: to pull an all-nighter, stay awake all night
parole.testo: From tras- + noche + -ar, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *trānsnoctāre, from trāns + nox (genitive singular noctis). Cognate with Galician trasnoitar, Asturian tresnochar.
From través + -ero, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *traversārius, from Latin trānsversārius, from trānsversus. Compare Portuguese travesseiro.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tractiāre, from Latin tractus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trāgella, from Latin trāgula.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trinitiāre, from trini.
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *triblāre, from syncopation of Latin tribulāre. Doublet of the borrowed tribular.

parole.significato: to shatter; to rip to shreds
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tritiāre, from Latin trītus + -āre. By surface analysis, triza + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *interpediāre, from *interpediō (“to impede”), from Latin inter- + pēs, pedis (“feet”) + -iō, perhaps formed analogously to impediō (“to impede”).
From Vulgar Latin tufus, from Late Latin typhus (“a type of fever”), from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos).

From alteration, with influence from turbio, of Old Spanish turbón (now dialectal), from Vulgar Latin *turbōnem (“whirlwind”), accusative of Latin turbinem, with altered declension. Compare Portuguese trovão (“thunder”), Galician trebón, torbón (“thunderstorm, downpour”). Doublet of turbina, from ul
Inherited from Old Spanish turbón (from Vulgar Latin *turbonem < Latin turbō) + -ada. See turbión.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ungla, from Latin ungula, from unguis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃negʰ-. Compare Portuguese unha.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vĭtīcula (“tendril of a plant”), from Late Latin vītīcula, from Classical Latin vītĭcula. First attested in 1438.
Inherited from Old Spanish vegada, from Vulgar Latin *vicāta, from Latin vicis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vēla, from the plural of Latin vēlum. Compare English veil.
Inherited from Old Spanish ventana, from Vulgar Latin *ventāna, from Latin ventus (“wind”) + -āna. Cognate with Asturian ventana, Galician ventá, and Portuguese ventã.

Inherited from Old Spanish verano (“spring”), from Vulgar Latin *(tempus) veranum, from Latin vēr (“spring”), from earlier *veror, from Proto-Italic *wezor, from Proto-Indo-European *wésr̥ (“spring”). Compare Portuguese verão.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viridizāre. Derivable from verde (“green”) + -ear (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: executioner, hangman (official person who carries out the capital punishment of a criminal)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *virdūcus, from *virde, from Latin viridis (“green”), with the meaning of "a green stick used to beat someone".
Inherited from Old Spanish verdura, from verde (“green”) + -ura (noun-forming suffix). Alternately, from Vulgar Latin *virdūra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *verrācus, from Latin verrēs (“boar”). Compare Romance cognates with varying suffixes: Portuguese barrão, Asturian verrón, French verrat, etc.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *verribundus, from Latin verrēs (“boar, male swine”) + -bundus.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; or possibly; modificatore <unc> nel legame
parole.testo: Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin root *virāre, of uncertain origin: possibly of Celtic; (compare Welsh gwyro) or possibly a variation of Latin vibrāre or gȳrāre. See also Portuguese virar, Italian virare.

parole.significato: sight, vision, eyesight (the ability to see)
parole.testo: From the Vulgar Latin *visita, from Latin videō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vīsitus, from Latin vīsus (“seen”) + -itus (regular perfect passive participle ending).

parole.significato: to upset, knock over, tip over, dump (to cause to flip over, from uppermost to bottom)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volvicāre, from Latin volvō (“to roll”). Compare Catalan bolcar.

From the feminine of the past participle of the verb volver (vuelto), or Vulgar Latin *volta, from *volŭta, from Latin volūta, from the feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Cognate with English vault and Italian volta.
Past participle of the verb volver; from Vulgar Latin *voltus, from *volŭtus, from Latin volūtus.

parole.significato: bed (a place to lie down in, especially one of low quality)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *iacilia, neuter plural of *iacīle, derived from Latin iacēre (“to lay”).
Inherited from Old Spanish yantar, from Vulgar Latin *iantāre (“to eat lunch”), from Latin iēntāre. See iēntāculum (“the first meal of the day”). Compare Portuguese jantar.
From a Vulgar Latin *erctus, past participle of *ergere, corresponding to Latin ērēctus < ērigere. Compare Italian erto. Doublet of erecto, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Old Spanish yedgo, from Vulgar Latin (Celto-Latin) *educus, from Gaulish odocos (influenced by or crossed with Latin ebulum).

Inherited from Old Spanish yunque, with metathesis from incue, itself from Vulgar Latin *incŭde, from Latin incūdem. The Old Spanish term, like the Latin etymon, was feminine. In the early modern period, a variant ayunque appeared, due to reanalysis with the article (la yunque > el ayunque), produci

From older çabullir, from Old Spanish çabollir, çobollir, from older sobollir, sebollir, sebellir, from Vulgar Latin sepellīre~*sepullīre (“bury”), from Latin sepelīre. First syllable appears to have been influenced by semantically-related words words such as zapuzar (“submerge”) and zahondar (“sink
Uncertain, but probably from an alteration of Vulgar Latin *strambus (“squinting, crosseyed, crooked, distorted”), from Latin strabus, from Ancient Greek στραβός (strabós).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sarcellum, diminutive of Latin sarculum (“hoe”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin ānsar, from Latin ānser, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns. Doublet of ganso.

From derezar, from Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre or *dērēctiāre, from Latin dīrēctus. Alternatively, via a Vulgar Latin *addīrēctiāre. Compare English address, Portuguese adereçar, French dresser, Asturian adrezar, Italian drizzare.

From older avenedizo, from Vulgar Latin *advenĭtīcius, a restructured form of Latin adventīcius. Doublet of adventicio. The first /d/ of modern advenedizo was probably taken either from adventicio or directly from Latin adventīcius.

parole.significato: to predict or announce something, especially a misfortune
parole.testo: Either from Vulgar Latin *agurāre, from Latin augurāre, in which case the maintenance of /o/ (and its diphthongization under stress) would be due to the influence of the noun agüero, or alternatively a verb independently built from the latter.
From almendra (“almond”), or from Vulgar Latin *amendlus < *amandulus, from Latin amygdalus, from Ancient Greek ἀμύγδαλος (amúgdalos), ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē). Compare Italian mandorlo.
From a- + luengo + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *allongāre, from Late Latin elongāre, from Latin longus.

From a- + parejo + -ar, or alternatively from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *appariclāre, contraction of *appariculāre, itself probably from Latin apparāre. Compare Portuguese aparelhar, Italian apparecchiare, French appareiller.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish arrufar, of uncertain origin. First attested c. 1250 in the sense "to become conceited". Said originally to have been borrowed from a Germanic language, compare English ruffle or Icelandic hrufla. However, it is difficult for a word mostly attested in northern Europe to tr

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; either; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Cognate with Portuguese baço, but uncertain origin. Probably either: * From Vulgar Latin *hepatium, from Ancient Greek ἧπατιον (hêpation), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”). * According to the Royal Spanish Academy, from Latin badius (“reddish brown”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Probably; perhaps; or from
parole.testo: From Old Spanish briza, thence of uncertain origin. Probably from Old French bise, bize, or from Vulgar Latin *bize, in which case likely of Germanic origin. Conversely, the French word has also been connected with Vulgar Latin *brevidia, whence probably Italian breva (“periodic wind around the lake

parole.significato: a small single-edged knife; a pocketknife
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish canyuete, canivete (1291), either from Old Occitan and Old Catalan canivet, ganivet (“small knife”) (Catalan ganivet), both from Vulgar Latin *cnīfittus (“small knife”), from Vulgar Latin *cnīfus (“knife”), from Frankish *knīf (“knife”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European

Uncertain. Possibly from a derivation of Vulgar Latin *cochleare, from Latin cochlea, from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías, “spiral, snail shell”). See also cuchara. Alternatively, possibly of pre-Roman substrate origin. Cognate with Portuguese caracol, Galician caracol, Asturian caracol, and Occita
From carniza + -ero or from Vulgar Latin *carniceārius, from Latin carō.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *carudium, from Ancient Greek καρύδιον (karúdion), from κάρυον (káruon, “nut”); alternatively, from a substrate language: compare carolo. Cognate with Portuguese caroço, Galician carozo. Doublet of garojo, which was inherited via a different development.
Either derived from casta (“caste”) + -izo or casto (“pure”) + -izo. Less likely inherited from a Vulgar Latin *casticeus, from Latin castus (“pure”).

parole.significato: fence (a thin artificial barrier that separates two pieces of land or a house perimeter)
parole.testo: Deverbal from cercar, or from Old Spanish cerca, from a Vulgar Latin *circa (compare Portuguese cerca, northern Italian cerca, French cerce), from the feminine of Latin circus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plattus (“flattened”), from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús). Given that this word is attested rather late in time, such as in Cervantes' Don Quixote of 1605, it's theorized that it may have been borrowed from Portuguese (where the phonetic shift of the Latin consonant clus

Inherited from Latin cingulum, through a syncopated Vulgar Latin form *cinglum, with palatalization of the 'l'. However, this phonetic evolution for Spanish presents difficulties to some linguists, who prefer a Vulgar Latin form *cīnctulum, influenced by cīnctum, the supine of the related verb cingō
Inherited from Old Spanish cirugiano, derived from cirugía, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *chirurgianus, from Latin chirurgia, from chirurgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin coda, from Latin cauda, or from its diminutive caudula. Cognate to French queue, Catalan cua, Aragonese coda and Italian coda.

parole.significato: pair of compasses (tool used to draw circles)
parole.testo: Apparently from Old French compas, perhaps from Medieval Latin compassus (“circle, circuit”), or the medieval Latin term is derived from Old French. In either case, deverbal from Vulgar Latin *compassāre (“to pace off”), from com- + *passāre (“to step”), from Latin passus (“step”), originally the pe
Either deverbal from conquistar or from a Vulgar Latin *conquīsta, from the feminine of Latin conquīsītus. Compare Portuguese and Italian conquista, French conquête.

Possibly from a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *conquīsītāre, from Latin conquīsītus, perfect passive participle of conquīrō; alternatively, it may simply be an internal formation, as a derivation of conquista, from the feminine past participle of Old Spanish conquerir, which this verb replaced over time
From cuadro + -illo, or from Vulgar Latin *quadrellus, from Latin quadrus. Compare Italian quadrello, French carreau.

parole.significato: a cone made of paper or other material and used to contain candy or other small items
parole.testo: From dialectal Italian cucuruccio (“conical hood, cone”), from an intermediate Vulgar Latin *cuculullius (“cone, cowl”), from Latin cucullus (“hood, cowl, conical wrapper”). Shared origin with English cowl. An ultimate Celtic origin, either borrowed from, into, or influencing the Vulgar Latin form i

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cova, from covus, alternative form of Latin cavus (or from a variant of Late Latin cava, from cavum, cavus), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówHwos (“cavity”). Compare Portuguese cova. Not related to English cove, despite the similarity in meaning.
From cuño or from Vulgar Latin *cunea, from Latin cuneus. Compare Portuguese cunha.

From a Vulgar Latin *dadu, of uncertain origin; perhaps from Arabic أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād, “numbers”), or alternatively from Latin dātum. Compare Portuguese dado, Catalan dau, Italian dado. Cf. also French dé.
From de- + ramo + -ar, or from a Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Romanian dărâma, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Italian diramare, Portuguese derramar.

Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *discalceus, itself either from a shortening of discalceātus, from Late Latin discalceō, or from Latin dis- + calceus. Cognate with Galician descalzo, Portuguese descalço, Catalan descalç, Occitan descauç, French déchaux, Italian scalzo and Romanian desc
From Late Latin or Vulgar Latin disligāre, from Latin dis- + ligō (“tie, bind”), or from deligāre. Alternatively formed from des- + liar, which may have been taken from or influenced by French.
From des- + torcer, or from Vulgar Latin *distorcēre, from Latin distorquēre.

From Latin duplus or duplex; if from the former, it is uncertain whether it was inherited or not, and may have been taken from a Catalan or Provençal intermediate, as the final '-e' rather than '-o' is unexpected. If from the latter, it is possible that it came from a Vulgar Latin *duplem as a varia
From en- + boca + -ar, or possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca (compare French emboucher, Italian imboccare, Romanian îmbuca).

From en- + cabestro (“halter”) + -ar, or alternatively a Vulgar Latin root *incapistrāre, from Latin capistrāre. Compare Portuguese encabrestar, Catalan and Occitan encabestrar, French enchevêtrer, Italian incapestrare, Sardinian incrabistare, Romanian încăpăstra.
From en- + derezar, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctiāre or *dīrēctiāre, from Latin dīrēctus. Compare Italian drizzare. Alternatively, from *indīrēctiāre. Cf. Portuguese endereçar, Italian indirizzare.
From gula, or from a Vulgar Latin *ingullīre, from Latin gula. Compare Catalan and Portuguese engolir, Italian ingollare. Not cognate with English engulf, despite similar phonetics and meaning.

From enjambre + -ar or from Vulgar Latin exāminō, exāmināre, from Latin exāmen. Compare Portuguese enxamear, Catalan eixamar, French essaimer, Italian sciamare.

parole.significato: to spy, to spy on (act as a spy)
parole.testo: From espía + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *spiāre, from Gothic or Frankish *spehōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).
Possibly from French fraise (“milling cutter”), or from the verb fresar, from Vulgar Latin *frēsāre, from frēsum, perfect passive participle of Latin frendō (“to grind”).

From fresa (“endmill”) + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin frēsare, frequentative of Latin frendere (“to grind”) through its past participle frēsum. The main sense of "to mill" was probably taken French fraiser.

From hoja, or from a Vulgar Latin *foliola, from Latin folium. Compare Galician filloa, folloa, Portuguese filhó.

parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ordiniāre, itself from Latin ōrdināre, or from *ordinium, from ōrdō, ōrdinis. Compare Portuguese ordenhar, Sardinian ordinzare; cf. also Italian ordigno. Doublet of ordenar.

From either Catalan or Occitan peltre, from Vulgar Latin *piltrum, of uncertain ultimate origin. Compare Portuguese peltre.

Inherited from Latin pertinēre (from whence a rare older Spanish pertener), with the suffix -ecer, or possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *pertinēscēre. Compare Portuguese pertencer. Related to pertain and pertinent.

From pinza + -ón. Alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *pincio, pincione, possibly of Celtic origin (compare French pinson, Italian pincione), or from an onomatopoetic root *pink-, with similar forms found in other European languages.
From piojo (“louse”) + -oso, or possibly from Vulgar Latin peduclosus, from Latin pēduculōsus.

From pollo, or from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of Latin pullus. Compare Catalan polla, French poule, Romanian pulă.

From a Vulgar Latin root *remussicāre, itself an alteration of *remussitāre, from Latin mussitāre, or from mussō. Compare Portuguese resmungar.
From re- + torcer, or from Vulgar Latin *retorcēre, from Latin retorquēre. Cognate with English retort.
From re- + volcar, or from a Vulgar Latin *revolvicāre, from Latin revolvō.
From an earlier *ruino, from ruina, or from a Vulgar Latin root *ruīnus, ultimately from Latin ruīna. Compare Portuguese ruim, Catalan roí. The lack of a final /-o/ may suggest a borrowing.

parole.testo: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *sagīnum, from Latin sagīna. To explain the absence of a final vowel, Coromines posits a borrowing from either Leonese, where /-inu/ > /-in/ is common, or Aragonese, where loss of final /o/ is common.
